That this House instructs the Solicitor General to make a statement on motions today explaining the serious contradiction which exists between his description of what was burned on June 3 and the statement made by Chief Superintendent Guy Marcoux yesterday and also to explain the circumstances which led to the report making the recommendation for the burning of these documents being prepared on May 23 of this year which was the Monday of a long holiday weekend.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to present a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, namely the Prime Minister's statement in Hamilton yesterday to the effect that "the Canadian Steel Industry will have to be competitive if it expects its steel pipe to be used on the Canadian portion of the Alaska-Yukon natural gas pipeline."
In view of the fact that Canada has provided the United States with a land bridge to bring United States gas from Alaska to that country thereby saving it $6 billion compared to the only other route under consideration, and in view of the fact that one of the few benefits accruing to Canada from this project is the commitment of Foothills (Yukon) Ltd. that all pipe will be purchased in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House calls upon the federal government to make it clear that it intends to hold Foothills (Yukon) Ltd. to its commitment and that it will insist that all the steel pipe used in the Canadian portion of the proposed pipeline will be produced in Canada in order to provide employment for Canadian workers.

I understand that the documents do go up to the period 1972-1973-I would have to check as to the exact date. I remind the House once again that there is a whole series of documents within the force, as in any other government department, with respect to which a normal policy of destruction is followed. 1 indicated at that time that the destruction which took place in Montreal had been carried out further to an audit which had

speakeroldname: Hon. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: ACTION TO PREVENT FURTHER BREACHES OF CONFIDENTIALITY OF TAX RETURNS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to repeat that we have tightened the security and are trying to find out where that particular problem is. When I do, Mr. Speaker, I shall let you know.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER INFORMED MINISTER OF BREACHES OF CONFIDENTIALITY OF TAX RETURNS

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER INFORMED MINISTER OF BREACHES OF CONFIDENTIALITY OF TAX RETURNS
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Will the minister indicate to the House whether the Prime Minister, who was contacted before the broadcast, has informed him of the communication from Messrs. Templeton and Berton that was also conveyed to the Leader of the New Democratic Party before the broadcast, so that they on that side of the House may co-operate with the authorities to get to the bottom of this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER INFORMED MINISTER OF BREACHES OF CONFIDENTIALITY OF TAX RETURNS
speechtext: As I said before, Mr. Speaker, 1 was only alerted to this this morning. We are acting accordingly and as quickly as we possibly can. If the hon. Leader of the Opposition had known about it before why did he not bring it to my attention? By now I would have had an answer for him.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: MR. CLARK-STATEMENTS OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a brief question of privilege relating to some of the recent statements of the Minister of National Revenue who has tried to excuse his conduct of the affairs of his department.
I should simply like to put on the record of the House a certain chronology of events.
I am sure the minister, being the competent minister he is known to be across the country, will already have read the transcript of the remarks of Mr. Berton and Mr. Templeton. He will know that the contact with me was made before there was verification of the contents of the particular file relating to me. I became aware of the verification this morning at roughly 11.15, an hour and ten minutes after the matter was broadcast.
I am told that the Prime Minister's office was advised well before that time.
If the Minister of National Revenue wants to inquire why members of parliament who became aware of this matter did not bring it directly to the attention of the government itself, perhaps he should deal directly with the office of his leader to find out why they did not advise him before the matter was broadcast.

subsubtopic: MR. CLARK-STATEMENTS OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was Acting Prime Minister this morning, and nobody informed me of anything until the Minister of National Revenue-

subsubtopic: MR. CLARK-STATEMENTS OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. CLARK-STATEMENTS OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext: They do not want to know the truth. The Minister of National Revenue informed me of the problem. I had a meeting with him and his officials in the cabinet room, and I have given all the facts to this House. What is extremely important is for everyone involved in a situation like this to act immediately. No one can reproach the Minister of National Revenue, the deputy minister or other officials who did not know anything about it. I asked the RCMP if anyone had informed them, and I am informed they knew nothing about it. If the hon. mumber learned anything about it before this morning, I should like to know. If not, I am happy it is not as some people have said, that perhaps he knew about it before. I accept his word that he did not know anything about it before this morning. I am very satisfied, but that is not what somebody has led me to believe.

subsubtopic: MR. CLARK-STATEMENTS OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE
speechtext: You accept my word?

Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a very important question of privilege inherent in the answer given by the Acting Prime Minister to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. I shall be very brief, but that does not mean it is not a very important question.
The question of ministerial responsibility is one which this government has sought to bring forward to defend its actions over the last tumultuous two weeks. As I interpreted the answer of the Minister of Finance, as leader of the government in this House today, he is saying it is adequate, to meet the charge of ministerial responsibility, for a minister to appear before a body outside this House, a body appointed by the government and with terms of reference established by the government. He says it is adequate for a minister to meet the question of ministerial responsibility by answering to that body.
I suggest to Your Honour that the powers and privileges of this House have been sadly reduced over the last eight or ten years by this government. One of the few left should surely be the right to demand that this House, on behalf of the people of Canada, may hold a minister accountable on the basis of ministerial responsibility.
If what the Acting Prime Minister has said is to be taken at its face value-it was a direct answer to a direct question- that has gone by the board. If that is the case, then I suggest

November 17, 1977

we in this House are entitled to know it. I would think that the Acting Prime Minister must be prepared-if not now, certainly within the next day or so-to let this House know if that is the way the government views the question of responsibility. If, in their view, it is sufficient that a minister can go to some outside body and in secret, if necessary, give testimony and meet the question of ministerial responsibility, then this House might as well pack up and go home.
Right on.

Mr. Speaker, I have been endeavouring to get the floor on what I was going to call a point of order. It is closely related to the issue raised by the hon. member for Peace River, however, so perhaps I could endeavour to make now the point of order I have in mind.
Several times during the question period interest and concern were expressed in the statements made outside the House by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs regarding matters that related to his former responsibility as a solicitor general. Members have tried to avoid offending the rule that says we cannot ask ministers questions relating to something for which they are not now responsible, and yet parliament seems to have been put in this position-supreme though we are, as we tried to say yesterday in another connection-that we cannot do on the floor of the House what a reporter can do outside the House.
It seems to me that somehow or other a way ought to be found for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to make a statement to this House concerning the matters that were within his knowledge when he was solicitor general, particularly in view of his statements outside the House. I am fully aware of the rule, and Your Honour has to guard it very carefully, but I would point out that upon occasion, usually after consultation with the House leaders of all parties, variations in the procedures have been made to meet a particular situation. One that came to mind when I was thinking about this matter, and which I looked up, occurred during the course of what was called the judges' affair. On two occasions during those days, once on March 12, 1976, and again on March 16, 1976, after consulting with the House leaders Your Honour varied the rule respecting motions made under Standing Order 43. [DOT]
I am not trying to say that Your Honour varied the rule about questioning ministers on things which were their former responsibility, but Your Honour did vary another rule because the House was particularly concerned about the matters then being discussed.
On March 12, instead of waiting until three o'clock Your Honour permitted the hon. member for Westmount, the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations and the Minister of Finance to make statements which had no relation to matters which were then part of their responsibilities. The
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
House was concerned. Then statements were made by hon. members on this side of the House.
On March 16, 1976, when the Minister of State for Urban Affairs had resigned that morning from his position as minister of consumer and corporate affairs, he was permitted not only to make a statement but he was permitted to make it at a time reserved for motions under Standing Order 43. It was at the end of that statement that he told us his resignation had been submitted that morning. We agreed to that, and comments were made afterwards. My point is: the rules, practices and procedures of the House were varied, by consent, because the House had a particular interest in the matters then being discussed.
There is no doubt of the interest of the House these past few weeks with respect to matters related to the RCMP and to the relationship between that body and the Solicitor General. Now we have a minister of the Crown making statements outside the House that are extremely relevant to the whole situation, and yet somehow or another our rules seem to prevent us from asking him questions or getting any information out of him. To say he will appear before the McDonald commission of inquiry is not very satisfactory. It is not recognizing the supremacy and the importance of this House. We have not even had the assurance that he will appear before a committee. Even that would not meet the immediate interest of the House of Commons.
My point of order is that surely common sense calls for us to have at least the rights in this House which reporters have outside. I would ask Your Honour to consult the House leaders of the various parties to see if an arrangement can be made for this interest of the House to be met in order for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs either to make a statement and be questioned after it, or be questioned with respect to matters within his knowledge because of the responsibility that he held for them.
I am happy to raise this point of order in association with the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Peace River, because I think his concern regarding what has happened to ministerial responsibility is very serious and very important. I think we should do something about it and not let our procedures stymie us completely.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be able to make a submission with respect to this matter. As I tried to say in the submission I made in the question and the preamble to the question, earlier in the question period the Minister of Finance, when talking about the incident referred to by the Solicitor General in his statement outside the House, inferred in his answer that it was one isolated matter of an accusation made by the former solicitor general against the RCMP, that they had in fact lied to him on one occasion. That was the inference.
In any event, it is very clear from the newspaper clippings and from what I saw on CTV last night that it was more than one incident. I attempted to quote what the Solicitor General

November 17, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
said about what the RCMP had either said or failed to say to him, which was a pretty strong accusation against the police. He said, "It seems to me that they did withhold information from me and from other solicitors general". Because there seemed to be some discrepancy concerning what was being said by a minister who did not make a statement outside the House with respect to a statement made outside the House, or purported to have been made outside the House, I asked him not to comment on his answer as to the truth or not of the statements attributed to him, but whether, as a member of the ministry, he would take advantage of the opportunity provided him by the rules of this House to come to the House and make a statement. If he came to the House and made a statement, there would be opportunity to question him specifically with respect to that which was contained in the statement. That was the purport of the question.
I realize Your Honour has to make instant judgments, but you did rise in your place and that question was not answered. Therefore, at this moment we do not know whether a minister of the Crown is prepared to come forward and give us the details surrounding those statements made by him outside the House about which there has been some confusion today on the floor of the House of Commons.
Perhaps I put it to Your Honour inarticulately, but I attempted to indicate that I was asking the minister a question in his capacity as a member of the government. During the judges' affair the hon. member for Westmount was questioned, as a member of the government, with respect to incidents which did not fall under his then ministerial responsibility. Yesterday in the House of Commons the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby asked a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It concerned a matter which the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that it would be drawing rather a long bow to have the answer to the question in his ministerial capacity. It is on that basis-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is dealing with a point which concerned me, as well, yesterday. Perhaps I should clarify that for the House. As the hon. member has said, I am required to make instant judgments, but yesterday the preamble to the quesion began with some reference to negotiations by the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs over the weekend. I have not verified the record, but that was the beginning of the question.
With that in mind, of course I had no way of knowing whether the negotiations referred to were domestic negotiations concerning the minister's political area of activity, or whether they were in fact ministerial in nature. Until the minister rose in an attempt to answer, I was not sure. Therefore, I could not tell from the question what area of responsibility was involved.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order for the House to understand the situation, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby is reported in Hansard as saying the following:

As the minister knows, the House is currently debating a bill which gives about $1 billion in tax concessions to corporations ostensibly to create jobs.
That was the preamble to the hon. member's question which was directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. My point is that that question was allowed.
Right on.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It was allowed in the same way, and for the same reasons, as the questions were allowed a year or so ago to the hon. member for Westmount when he was involved in the judges' affair which ultimately, and unfortunately, led to his resignation from the ministry.
It is within my capacity as a member of this House to ask a minister of the Crown whether or not he is prepared to make a statement. I am not asking him to make a statement in answer to my question. I consider a ruling on that to be extremely important, because I want to pose that question once again to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, if I can, and perhaps to the Minister of Supply and Services because he is the other solicitor general referred to.
I would like to know whether or not they are willing to make statements in the House with respect to the allegations which have been made against the RCMP concerning the way the RCMP conducted itself in relation to members of the ministry. If the statement of the minister outside the House is true, then some heads should roll in the RCMP. However, if that statement is not true, the minister has a course of action open to him. He will have carried out, albeit outside the House, an action which would indicate that his statements are not in accordance with the facts. This House has to know the facts before the McDonald commission knows them.
I believe it is important that I be allowed to put the question. As a result of it, I hope the minister will make a statement so he can be questioned with regard to that statement. So that Your Honour will be forewarned, I would like to put the same question to the Minister of Supply and Services. If there is one place where we ought to be able to question ministers, it is here. If there are to be restrictions on the right of members to question ministers-and I am prepared to admit there should be from time to time-we ought to lean against that to the greatest extent possible.
The whole purpose of this parliament is to be able to ask ministers questions directly as events occur. If we are to wait for the royal commission, the RCMP and the officers who are not now named by the Minister of Supply and Services will remain under a cloud. That is a fact, a fact that this House ought not to allow to exist in terms of any public servant of the government.

Mr. Speaker,
I would like to make a few comments on this question of privilege. I am pleased that the hon. member is afraid that someone can cast doubt on a civil servant. I wish he had
November 17, 1977

developed that philosophy two weeks ago when they started making accusations.
Oh, oh!

Under the circcumstances, I think the rule is clear. When a question concerning a particular department is asked, it is the responsible minister who must reply to that question in the House. The Solicitor General was willing to answer questions, and in fact has done so. In my capacity as Acting Prime Minister today, I spoke with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in my office. We discussed the matter and I asked whether he made those accusations. He told me that he referred to an incident that was debated in the House. He gave it as an example. He did not intend to make any accusations against the RCMP.
I have followed the rules of this House. Perhaps members opposite find these rules somewhat restraining. However, we have to abide by the rules and practices of this House. Sometimes they are also restraining for members on this side. It is often difficult for a parliamentary secretary to get the floor to ask questions because he has accepted some responsibility. For the past 10'/2 years that I have been a minister I have had to forgo my right to ask questions on behalf of my constituents who elected me. However, that is one of the rules we have to live with.
This morning we did exactly what has been done under similar circumstances over the years, that is ask the minister what comments he made. I reported to the House what the minister said to me. I said that if there are other questions related to this matter, they can be asked of the Solicitor General. I can appreciate the frustrations of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, but that is the price one must pay when serving another department. He can no longer answer for the previous department for which he had responsibility. If a member wishes to ask some questions about a minister's former responsibility, he must do that through the Prime Minister or the Acting Prime Minister. That is the rule, and we are obliged to abide by it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to give quite briefly my opinion on this issue which is, I feel, very serious indeed. In view of the fact that this report was seen by millions of Canadian taxpayers who submit every year their income tax returns, with the assurance that the information they provide is treated as extremely confidential-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bellechasse is dealing with an entirely different subject, for the House is now considering the possibility of a statement the hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) might make concerning a question and answer exchange which took place in Montreal last night. That is one thing. The second concerns income tax returns and their confidential nature: that is something completely separate.
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin

I wish to thank you for your decision, Mr. Speaker. That was my preamble. What I mean to say is this: the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) came up with a wise suggestion a while ago, a suggestion with which I fully agree, and I feel that the minister should be given the opportunity to provide the House with full explanations, even if he should require a whole hour to do so, in such a way that this institution may be truly recognized by the public as really responsible.
As far as House leaders are concerned, I feel that we should meet and discharge very wisely our responsibilities. If the minister wants to explain his conduct to the House, he ought to be given the time he needs, which would clarify the situation and rekindle the faith the Canadian people have always had in the Parliament of Canada.
[English)

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak briefly to this very important question now before the House. I listened, as the House did, with great interest to the Acting Prime Minister. I say to him, through you, sir, with respect that 1 do not think he understands the gravity or the seriousness of the question before the House. If the good name of the RCMP which has been dragged down in the mud by his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, is to be cleared of this unprecedented smear by a minister, what better place to do that than here in the House?
Hear, hear!

It could be done in the House on a statement on motions or on a question of privilege by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. That is precisely what the House leader of the official opposition was asking, and the point the House leader for the New Democratic Party was getting at. The central question here, and I say this with great respect, is that of the collective responsibility of ministers of the Crown. Last evening the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, as reported over national television, referred to several instances when he was solicitor general and, indeed, referred as well to his predecessor and where he had been given misinformation or information had been withheld from him by the RCMP.
The only way the House has to get at this matter today, according to the ruling of Your Honour, which I respect, is by way of questions to the Acting Prime Minister. The Acting Prime Minister then told the House that on the basis of a conversation he had with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs it is an entirely different situation and there is only one particular instance that was referred to. We have two stories. One was given to the press and reported over national television by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who has not been given an opportunity by Your Honour to report to the House, and the other story was given today by the Acting Prime Minister on behalf of his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.

November 17, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
I realize Your Honour has to make instant judgments from day to day. This is a very serious question. It has seized the attention of the House for the last number of weeks. What we are getting at here is the question of collective responsibility of ministers of the Crown in dealing with a question before the House which has to do with, not one but three ministers still in the cabinet who were responsible for this very question, namely, the question of their dealings with the RCMP on matters of national security.
We are not trying to get at former ministers of the Crown. We are not trying to deal with a minister of the Crown on the basis of his constituency responsibilities, as was the case yesterday in the question put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. If you examine the record, you will find it dealt purely and simply with a matter within the jurisdiction of the minister by virtue of his position in this House as the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. There is no way in which the question could have been permitted except on that basis. But we are not getting at that.
I can understand that Your Honour would perhaps wish to reflect further on that question by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby so that a dangerous precedent might not be set. But the precedent is well established that ministers of the Crown are collectively responsible and accountable to the House for their actions. However, serious charges have been made, in the presence of the press, by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the former solicitor general- charges which, if substantiated, would result in severe disciplinary action being taken against members of the RCMP; and if they cannot be substantiated, the minister would have only one honourable course to follow, which is to resign.
So there is also the question of the serious charges which have been made by a minister outside this House against the RCMP whose name has been smeared without any substantiation, and I submit that the House should be given an opportunity to hear from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs either by way of a statement on motions or by way of a question of privilege, so that the good name of the RCMP can be cleared in this House by a minister who has smeared it outside the House.

Mr. Speaker, there is one aspect of this matter which has not so far been covered. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, speaking in Montreal, used the words "solicitors general" in the plural form. I take it he was not referring only to his immediate predecessor but to his successor, the present Solicitor General. Is he implying that the present Solicitor General is being misled by his officials?
We want to have confidence in the statements the present Solicitor General makes in the House, and this is hardly possible if there are suspicions that he is being misled by his officials. If the Acting Prime Minister refers this matter to the commission, it will take months before anything is done. What

will we do in the meantime while this lack of confidence exists, and what will the RCMP do in the meantime? They can put up no defence for themselves.
We wish to continue to place confidence in the statements made by the Solicitor General. Are we to live under this shadow in the months ahead while statements made by the Solicitor General are under a cloud, as well as the RCMP? I would, therefore, ask Your Honour to rule in favour of the submission made by my leader and by my hon. friend for Grenville-Carleton.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that, as so frequently happens, the opposition is basing even the preliminaries of its case upon a report of something which was said outside the House. I would point out that one of the ordinary functions of hon. members opposite is to deal with questions asked directly of ministers in relation to matters which are within their responsibility. Many of us acting in political capacities speak on subjects of many kinds across the country, and it would be quite impossible to deal with those matters in this House.
The issue is this: can questions be put here in relation to matters about which the opposition wishes to ascertain facts? Clearly, they can. The minister can be asked whether there are any new accusations against the Mounted Police: that question could have been directed to the Solicitor General. If the opposition is making an allegation of conduct unbecoming a minister, that is a matter which obviously goes to the Prime Minister or to the Acting Prime Minister. In that case, though, it would as well if they had the full facts, rather than simply basing their position on a press report. I think this is part of our difficulty, this practice of basing questions on what is reported in the press instead of asking questions directly in order to seek information or to determine responsibility.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
With all due respect to the Minister of Transport, Mr. Speaker, I think he has missed the point altogether. The question of privilege is not one which deals specifically with press reports. What the hon. member for Peace River and others were dealing with was an answer given by the Acting Prime Minister in which he contended that a former minister can avoid questions in the House of Commons and still give evidence before a royal commission related to matters which had come before him during his tenure of office as solicitor general. He can give evidence before the commission, but we are to be denied the opportunity of hearing him in the House of Commons which, after all, is the supreme commission and the highest court in this country.
The point is whether or not, now that we have made provision in our rules for a minister or for an ex-minister to stand in his place and make a statement related to circumstances which occurred during his tenure of office, we are to be prevented from asking questions even if he is prepared or has the courage to face his peers in this chamber and face the Canadian people. Alternatively, is parliament to have no ability to deal with this issue? Is it one which can be circumvented
November 17, 1977

by the Prime Minister shifting his cabinet around every few months so that no one is accountable for any significant period of time? That is the crux of the situation. We must have the opportunity of addressing ourselves to the issue before the House. The issue of ministerial responsibility involved here is one which transcends the limitations of cabinet portfolios held at a particular time; it is one which does not merely concern one particular portfolio or another.
I grant that the Prime Minister has an overriding capacity in this regard, but when it comes down to the question of ministerial responsibility, to accusations made by a former minister against the public servants under his guidance over a period of time, we ought to have the right to ask that minister to clarify his position or, if he does not, to resign.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this, a point of order rather than a question of privilege in my view, I would simply like to say a few words to stress what has been recognized by the other side, namely that we have a rule under which a minister does not have to answer questions relating to matters of administration for which he was formerly responsible. Such is the rule, and we must abide by it.
And since the Royal Commission of Inquiry has apparently been taken to task for holding certain privileges, I would like through you, Sir, to remind the House that in the preamble to Privy Council's decision dated July 6, 1977 establishing that Royal Commission, it was provided that the commissioners were appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act. Sections 4 and 5 of that act specifically give commissioners the power of summoning before them any witnesses, and this includes ministers of the Crown. Therefore, in view especially of the last point the last speaker tried to make, I see no reason why the Royal Commission of Inquiry should be taken to task for having that privilege of calling witnesses, because here in this House the minister cannot be questioned on matters of administration for which he is not now responsible. The rules are there. While they may not be perfect, I submit we should not try to change them one by one, as and when we find this advisable from a partisan standpoint.
There is room in this House, as has been advocated for a long time, for in-depth reform. I feel that such changes should be considered in a perfectly objective way, in a totally non-partisan context. Once more, I respectfully submit that what opposition parties have today is a point of order rather a question of privilege. Our rules are clear. A minister does not have to make a statement on matters of his former responsibility. If opposition parties feel they should complain about rules, we on this side are prepared to consider changes of a general nature in various other areas, such as reducing the length of speeches, shortening the parliamentary week schedule from five to four days in order that members may have more time to look after constituency matters. All such changes should in my view be considered in a completely non-partisan context.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would simply note that the opposition feel it is in their interest to rescind the rule prevent-
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
ing a minister from answering questions that pertain to matters of his former responsibility. They would welcome that, because they believe this could be profitable from a partisan point of view. I doubt this would be the case. If, however, changes are desired, we are prepared to discuss them, not in a piece-meal, unruly way, but in good faith and in a totally non-partisan context.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peace River has raised, by way of a question of privilege, a difficulty that has faced us on occasion before. I would like to consider the arguments which have been put forward. I think hon. members will realize, however, that there is a fundamental difficulty for the Chair, in the circumstances, and that is that there is no relief which can be ordered by the Chair. Previous occasions have been cited and there have been applications from both sides to attempt to vary the rules in order to accomplish a certain purpose. In the face of those applications, there are certain things that can be done.
There are other circumstances with which I have been faced: motions attempting to deal with a certain circumstance in a given way. However, at the moment I have no application for specific relief, and it is very difficult for the Chair to invent actions which can be taken and which might attempt to provide relief in certain circumstances. I do confess to some difficulty, as hon. members have expressed today-and this is one of the things I will want to consider-that in the circumstances members of the House are confined in their questions to the current and present ministerial responsibility of each incumbent of a ministerial portfolio. That is clearly understood and no one will put that at issue today. That doctrine is strained greatly when a minister takes advantage outside this House to make statements-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: -about previous ministerial responsibilities. It seems to me that if that doctrine is to prevail, then those responsibilities, if anything is going to be said about them, ought to be said by the present incumbent of that portfolio in order that it can be reported to the House. But, in any case, that is a rather gratuitous observation which I hope is germane to some of the arguments which were presented today. I will want to reserve on this, but I thought before doing so, I might expose to the House some of the difficulties that I face. I will try to be of as much assistance to the House in this matter as I can and rule on the matter in a more definitive way tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question on behalf of the tourist industry in Canada, which is experiencing serious economic difficulties. I had a short preamble to explain my question, and then the next thing I knew, you rose to cut me off when I started my question, without any explanation. You recognized another

November 17, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Hogan
member across the way. If my preamble was too long, sir, 1 would certainly like it explained. I have watched this matter very closely and I have read questions in Hansard with regard to the length of preamble that certain members are allowed, especially the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I have watched with great interest over the past few months the length of time that he has been allowed to ask questions and make a preamble.
I have not abused the question period since the House resumed on October 18. This is only my second question, and I have had only one motion under Standing Order 43. If certain members are to have special privileges regarding the length of their preambles or the length of their questions, then I think we are entitled to an explanation, sir. I am going to rise tomorrow, and I am asking you now to recognize me tomorrow and allow me to ask my question. When you cut me off, you are cutting off the constituents of Winnipeg South Centre, the Canadian people and the travel industry.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must apply the same rule to all other members of the House in the situation to which the hon. member referred. He was given the floor, began his question, was permitted a preamble, and then proposed, it seemed to me, to read from a set of documents a resolution by an association. At that point I rose specifically to ask the member to put his question. The member continued, without reference to the fact I was on my feet.
In any case, as he was then moving to put his question, I sat down to permit him to do so. Instead of doing that, he turned around and faced the Chair with the words, "What's the problem?" That, it seems to me, was a somewhat disrespectful way to address the Chair in any circumstances. At that point I recognized another member, and not previously. I had no intention of stopping the member putting his question until he did that.

subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I notified you previously that I wished to raise this matter when the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was in the House. With your permission, I would like to do so now. In order to lay the basis for my question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, and in order to guide you in deciding whether I really have a question of privilege in fact, I have to quote briefly from Hansard of November 9, 1977, page 759.
We are slow in developing some of our coal mines. That is one aspect which could be improved.

subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext: Especially in Cape Breton.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext: Especially in Cape Breton because of the costs, and I think I should say perhaps because of the 'inappreciability' of the Cape Bretoner for the retention of his job. That is a serious accusation.

subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext: What's that?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Read it in Hansard.
Mr. Speaker, I want to distinguish between two things that the minister said about Cape Breton as far as the opening of the coal industry is concerned. If he had remained with a question of fact that because of high costs-as he implied in the past-it is very difficult to open new coal mines, then he is obviously correct and is correct up to this day. The federal government has, since 1927, because of high costs in connection with Cape Breton coal mines, given subventions to the private owners who own the coal industry. That was done until the federal government took over the industry under Devco in 1967. But I remind the hon. minister that costs are relative, and the minister in charge of DREE said in Edmonton two or three weeks ago, at a national coal conference, that he expected that by the end of this decade the coal mines in Cape Breton would be a viable economic operation.
I go further and suggest that if what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the head of the petroleum institute of Venezuela have been telling us is true, that we are possibly going to pay $20 a barrel for crude oil by 1987, then the price of Cape Breton coal will be low in comparison and the government will be making all kinds of money on the Cape Breton coal mines. That is not the question of privilege, but I wanted to make the distinction because of what the minister introduced as a question of fact.
My question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said that the inappreciability of Cape Bretoners for the retention of their jobs is one of the causes for not opening new coal mines. He said that in the House. This is a serious accusation. As is usual in this House, when the minister speaks, unless he is reading from a speech prepared by civil servants he gives no factual evidence for his straight from the lip, wild generalizations and accusations.
In fairness to the many Cape Bretoners who are unemployed, to the people of an historic area of Canada who have

fought a hard fight for economic security all through this century, with thousands of them having been killed or maimed for life in these coal mines, the minister owes this House, the citizens of Canada and the people of Cape Breton an explanation of his evidence for the statement "the 'inappreciability' of the Cape Bretoner for the retention of his job" as one of the reasons the government is slow in developing coal mines, especially in Cape Breton.
The minister should know there has been no major strike in the Cape Breton coalfields since 1947. The minister is a lover of free enterprise, and he should know that the days lost through illegal walk-outs at the Appalatian coalfields in the United States, which are privately owned, have been about 500 per cent higher, on a per capita basis, over the last five years than in the Cape Breton coalfields. I therefore challenge the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to back up his accusations with solid, factual evidence. I personally, am getting a little sick and tired of hearing him in this House acting-

subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext: I was speaking at length about the whole question of energy. I did mention we were slow in developing some of our coal mines and that is one aspect that has to be improved. I have long been a believer that more coal mines could be opened and developed in Cape Breton, particularly now that coal has to compete with highcost oil, not the 80-cent a barrel oil it was competing with a number of years ago. The hon. member was reading a statement and someone interrupted by saying "Especially in Cape Breton", and I agreed, especially in Cape Breton. I went on to refer to the extremely high cost in respect of some of the old underground mines. I should say, perhaps, that I spoke of the "inappreciability" of the Cape Bretoner. I want to point out to the hon. member that I did not say the "Cape Breton miner"; 1 said the Cape Bretoner generally.

subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext: And what does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
The hon. member now wants to know what I meant. I will tell him. I did not say the "inappreciability" of the Cape Breton miner; 1 said "the 'inappreciability' of the Cape Bretoner for the retention of his job"-"as a coal miner," I probably should have added. I was referring to jobs
Privilege-Mr. Hogan
as coal miners. Coal mining is a little bit like farming; some people look upon it as being the last job on earth that they would take. It is down at the bottom of the scale. The coal miner is often regarded as some kind of a serf in our society. I have never believed that. That is what I was referring to. The coal miner today should have a very noble place, particularly in coal mining areas such as Cape Breton. Nova Scotia now does not have as high a utilization of coal for the generation of electricity as it should. It does not have as high a utilization of coal for this purpose as does even the province of Alberta.
I was pleased to be down in Nova Scotia yesterday when the Premier of that province announced the opening of a new strip mine in that area which will take out an estimated one million tons of coal a year. I want particularly to bring that to the attention of hon. members. That will do much for the coal mining industry and the coal miner. In addition, on the mainland of Nova Scotia, the Wimpey Coal Company Limited, which is under contract to do strip mining of some coal there-and this government has encouraged both projects- will take out some thing like 400,000 tons of coal.
I should go on to say, in addition, Mr. Speaker, that this government has paid for drilling exploration off the coast of Nova Scotia and Cape Breton to find more, as well the depth and quantity of coal deposits in Cape Breton. Approximately three-quarters of the cost of that exploration has been paid for by this government, and the exploration results are very encouraging. It is my belief that more underground coal mines can be opened up which will be far more efficient than some of the old ones now in production.
Having said that, I hope I have cleared up any misunderstanding that might have been left by that remark in reference to "inappreciability". I was not referring to the coal miner but to the Cape Breton and Nova Scotia people, because to me it has been an appalling situation-

subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext: It is an appalling situation to me that the province of Nova Scotia generates 65 per cent to 85 per cent of its electricity through the use of imported, high-cost oil. More of the electricity should be developed through the use of coal, and I am pleased to see that the province is moving in that direction by opening up these two strip mines from which will be taken out a total of 1.4 million tons of coal per year for the development of electricity.

subsubtopic: MR. HOGAN-COAL INDUSTRY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. 1 did try to catch your eye at the time, but you allowed the minister to speak. I want to join wholeheartedly the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, who I think did a very good job. The minister, during his reply, squirmed, wiggled, twisted and turned all over the damned place and never did get around to explaining what he meant by "the inappreciability of the Cape Bretoner

November 17, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Hogan
for the retention of his job". He said he was not referring to the miner; he was referring to all Cape Bretoners. Then just before he concluded his remarks he said it was all Nova Scotians.
I proposed a motion under Standing Order 43 yesterday. I waited through Monday and Tuesday and the minister was not here. Some days back I raised the same question. He was very kind. I reminded him of having been my former seatmate, and told him of the problems of Cape Breton. I tried to tutor him on the problems of that area. He agreed that we have problems. He was very kind, yes. He said at that time he was aware of the problems of deep mines in Nova Scotia, as well as the strip mining, and said he would encourage the development of both, etc.
He said, in reply to another question, "My long association with the hon. member has made me very, very aware of the problems of Cape Breton. He can rest assured that the representation will be noted and remembered". Then he changed, on November 8, as the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton-East Richmond said-it is right in Hansard-and admitted this when he said, "That is a serious accusation". Well, if you are going to put your tongue in high gear when what little brain you have is still in park, you can expect statements like this.
Indeed, in addition to that I asked yesterday in my proposed motion whether the minister would make a public apology to the people of Cape Breton. My good friend who sits over there now should know what problems we have in Cape Breton. As one who has gone through a mine explosion, has been carried out of the mines twice and had his spine fractured in half a dozen places, I know what these men have gone through, as referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. There are miners suffering from pneumonomelanosis, silicosis, who have had arms and legs amputated, yet here we have a minister of the Crown who has the gall to make a statement such as he has made. He intimated that Cape Bretoners are lazy. Then he said it was not the Cape Breton
miner,	just Cape Bretoners; and he went on to say it was Nova Scotians. What can we take from that?
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, according to today's press, the minister was in a bearpit session last night at Dalhousie University where he reiterated, according to the press, his statement about the inappreciability of the Cape Breton coal miner for the retention of his job. In addition, the minister said that Cape Bretoners have an aversion to working in the coal
mines.	Is the hon. gentleman aware that the latest information from the personnel office of the Cape Breton Development Corporation shows there are between 3,000 and 4,000 applications for employment in the coal mines of Cape Breton, whether they are strip mines, deep mines or anything else? Is he not aware of that? If there is an aversion to working in the coal mines and guys do not want to work there, why would they be applying for jobs in the coal mines?
The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond and myself receive telephone calls, letters and other communications day after day from these people asking us to please find

them jobs in the coal mines. I want to know what this hon. gentleman is going to do with his great, strong, loud voice, shouting from the lip rather than the hip, to get us some more money so the Cape Breton Development Corporation can open up more mines. He talks about drilling. We know about that. We need more mines operating. We know about the strip mining, and that is okay as long as they replace the overburden; but there is no work on deck.
The minister certainly owes Cape Bretoners an apology. He talks about his dear friends in Cape Breton. From the reports I have been getting on the telephone, by radio and television, he has no friends in Cape Breton and will not unless he straightens out this matter. We are just a bunch of idiots down there, as far as he is concerned. We are lazy, and nobody will work. If this government will provide the work, there are plenty of people down there who will work.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was beginning to wonder whether I would manage to get the floor this afternoon, because I have a plane to catch in 40 minutes. But I still feel that I have something to contribute to this debate. When I called it six o'clock last evening, aside from the fact that it was 6.30 p.m., I was speaking about the size and depth of the borrowing authority which is being sought in this bill. I understand, although I am not a legislative lawyer, that there could be some question about trying to insert borrowing authority into a bill of this sort. I think that matter might be raised in the House by other members, or in committee of the whole.
The point I was making last night was that some $9 billion was being sought under this authority, and I offered to describe to hon. members just how much $9 billion was. I am not sure that we are all aware of how much it is; therefore, 1 made a few inquiries. According to my information, which is derived from the Bank of Canada, our bills are printed on paper which is three and three-quarter thousandths of an inch thick; that is, by my interpretation, .00375 of an inch. So I said to myself, suppose I had one $1,000 bill printed on the same kind of paper. I do not know how many people in the House have ever seen a $1,000 bill. I do not know that I have ever seen one. I see there are some members who have seen them: they are all on the other side. In any event, whether or not they have seen them, these bills are .00375 of an inch thick. If we were to put a thousand of these bills together into a pile amounting to $1 million, the pile would be 3.75 inches high.
That is not very much, but what about $1 billion? We would have to pile a thousand of those $1 million piles on top of each other, and if we were standing on the balcony around the Peace Tower and reached into the pile, we would be reaching into it at about two-thirds of the way up, but we could do so only if the pile did not tip over. We should not try to tip it over, because it would make a mess on the street below. Normally we consult Beauchesne with regard to our rules, but the same Arthur Beauchesne also wrote about Canada's Parliament Buildings and he described the Peace Tower in this way:
At approximately the two hundred foot level and opening of the clock chamber are four balconies-
I said that each $1,000 pile would be 3.75 inches high. If we multiply that by one thousand, we get 3,750 inches. If we divide that by 12, we get something in the order of 312 feet of $1,000 bills. At the 200-foot level of the Peace Tower we would be only two-thirds of the way up that pile. We are not talking today, however, about $1 billion; we are talking about the authority to borrow $9 billion, so we have to multiply by nine. How much is that? Instead of piling those bills up that way-because we could never keep the pile balanced-we

November 17, 1977

would have to lay it on its side, putting the packages on their edges and stretch it out that way. Those packages of $1,000 bills would stretch over half a mile across the countryside.
1 mentioned last evening that $9 billion was approximately the budget when this government came to power in 1968. Now it is asking for authority to borrow $9 billion because its indebtedness this year is going to be a little more than $9 billion. After ten years, this government is seeking to borrow an amount equal to $1 million packets stretched half a mile, standing on edge. That is a lot of money. On page 84 of the latest public accounts we can find the size of the national debt. We are going to add $9 billion to the national debt if this bill passes.
In 1968, when this government came to power, the national debt stood at $32 billion. In 1976, the last year for which figures are available, the national debt was $71.7 billion. When we reduce these figures to the per capita debt of each one of our constituents-not just the taxpaying constituents but even the small ones who do not yet have the right to vote- we find that the per capita debt in 1968 stood at over $1,500. Today, it stands at over $3,000. These figures are absolutely staggering; therefore, we must look very carefully at this provision. This is a request for borrowing authority to be found at page 210 of Bill C-ll. We must look at it very carefully before approving it, because the government is asking for what can only be described as phenomenal borrowing powers.
