speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to contribute to this debate, in keeping with the recent ruling handed down by that eminent jurist, Mr. Justice Evans, I ask Your Honour to keep strict and assiduous control of the television switches in this House. In case I make any culpable statements, privileged here but not beyond, i hope Your Honour will turn off that media so that the CBC or the CTV will not be sued in our courts of law for the illegal dissemination of my remarks.
For my opening remarks on this bill, I will go straight to the opening statement of the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) when he spoke on the bill last Monday, the seventh day of this month. As recorded at page 644 of Hansard for that date, the minister said:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-ll is now before the House for second reading. Its purpose is twofold: first, to implement amendments to the Income Tax Act as announced by myself on October 20 and as put forward by my predecessor, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), in his March 31 budget; second, to increase government borrowing authority.
To deal first with the second part of the minister's statement, I do not think anyone in this House can seriously consider extending this government's authority to borrow. This government has overborrowed. It has abused the use of taxpayers' money. It has overspent. The last thing we should be considering at this time, and the last thing which I, in all conscience, could agree to at this time would be to give this government carte blanche to push us further into debt. Any wage earner in Canada who manages his or her finances as poorly as this government does, or who has as much difficulty meeting payments on debts, would be the poorest risk for
Income Tax
making further loans. Such a person would have to be either a fool or a dreamer to think that any lending institution would advance more money-in effect, to throw still more money after bad.
This government should not be coming to this House for an extension of borrowing power, especially at this time when the state of our economy is sick. This government is already spending money we do not have, money that is not earned and in some cases money which has not yet been accounted for. Nowhere in the opening remarks of the Minister of Finance can I find one shred of justification for allowing the government to borrow more money. The minister brought his colleague, the former minister of finance, into his opening remarks, perhaps hoping that we had forgotten that the previous minister virtually wrecked the Canadian economy. He at least put the finishing touches to a national economy which has been going downhill steadily for the past seven or eight years. For this minister to suggest that he needs more borrowing power to finance programs initiated by the previous minister of finance is less than credible.
The minister really should have started from scratch unless, of course, he needs someone with whom to share his blame. When one observes the game of musical chairs the cabinet has been playing over the years, it seems that every minister of the Crown is constantly seeking someone with whom to share blame for this thing or that. If the cloud hanging over a minister gets too big or too heavy, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) simply shifts him sideways out of the portfolio and slides someone else in. One thing which can be said of the previous minister of finance is that he was so sure he was heading in the right direction that he just went on and on with his vehicle stuck in reverse until the Prime Minister finally steered him to the side of the road and got him out of the driver's seat. However, I might add that happened four or five years too late.
The Minister of Finance said in his speech that Bill C-ll is designed to increase government borrowing authority by $9 billion in new money-I repeat, $9 billion in new money. He was quick to add that this was in addition to the authority presently vested in the government to borrow to repay maturing debt. So all we are doing is trying to raise money to pay the interest on interest. That is very poor economics.
I wish the minister had taken the opportunity to bring us up to date on the present state of the gross national debt. That is something this House does not talk about enough, the state of our gross national debt. That is the load our children, our grandchildren and our great grandchildren will have to bear. Perhaps the minister will take this as notice and provide that information to the House in the course of the debate of Bill C-ll. I propose to speak of it later in my remarks. I know that the level of the national debt is shocking.
The minister stated that the government has relented in part and will not ask the tax collector to the graveside to collect proceeds of life insurance policies from survivors. The govern-

November 17, 1977
Income Tax
ment was fully prepared to do just that in the original draft of this legislation, as hon. members will recall. The government backed down to some degree following a barrage of protest from the official opposition and people all across the country. The efforts of the official opposition were largely responsible for the government backing down on the proposal to tax proceeds from life insurance policy death benefits. However, the government saw too much of a good thing, an easy grab, in the proceeds from life insurance policies to back off completely. While it has retreated from its previous ghoulish position at the graveside, it has not retreated from the field. It is still in the cemetery. I should like to return to this item later.
I should like to address myself again to the minister's opening statement and lay to rest the fiction that he is not planning to table a new budget. In response to repeated requests from the official opposition for a budget that would come to grips with unemployment and inflation, the tumbling Canadian dollar and a multitude of other economic woes, the Minister of Finance insists that a new budget is not needed at this time and is not forthcoming. What are we debating today, then? Is it a near budget, a mini-budget or pseudo budget? Call it what you will, it is a budget.
The Minister of Finance ties this bill directly to the budget tabled by the previous minister in March, 1977, according to his opening statement on November 7. I prefer to entitle this a pseudo budget, using the definition of the word contained in Webster's Seventh Collegiate Dictionary. The word "pseudo" is defined as "sham". It is a sham budget. The most we can expect is the government's own expectation of a $9 billion borrowing authority if this bill is passed-$9 billion further into debt. Yet the government denies that this is a budget. Perhaps the reason the minister will not call it a budget is that a budget is expected to contain provisions to improve the state of the economy and improve the lot of the average Canadian, usually coming at intervals of one parliament at a time. That is not the case here. Another reason is that a budget debate would open up new areas of discussion that the government would like to avoid. The fact remains that this is nothing but a sham budget.
To get back to the question of taxing the benefits of life insurance policies, life insurance in our society has always been the last refuge of the lower and middle income earners, in more ways than one. I am one of those, so I speak from experience. Life insurance is the best way for a poor person to save money. It always has been, and I hope it always will be, available to the Canadian people, untramelled and untouched by the long fingers of government. There is the all-important aspect of the death benefits which help the survivors to recover from the shock of losing a breadwinner as well as a loved one. This refuge is slowly being eroded by a government that is totally unfeeling and completely avaricious. The name of the game, where this government is concerned, is to reach out and grab, no matter what the consequences to the individual.
Another way in which life insurance has been a boon to the lowly paid wage earner has been the provision whereby a portion of the cash value of a policy that has been in effect for

a number of years can be borrowed, using the policy as security. Tens of thousands of policyholders through the years have used this provision to obtain money to ease them through a financial crisis.
Always on the lookout for a quick buck, the mandarins in the tax bureau have alerted the government to a so-called loophole which they say will yield so many million dollars in taxes if it is closed off. I refer to the alleged "gain" provision in the insurance policy loan provision, whereby the difference between the cash surrender value of a policy and the premiums paid is construed as income for tax purposes.
That is utter nonsense and does not stand up even under cursory examination. A loan is a loan, whatever the manner in which it is made, and it has to be repaid. If it is only for the amount of premiums paid, plus accrued interest, or if it is for an amount that is greater than the amount of premiums paid, it must be repaid at one time or another. The ultimate value of a life insurance policy is the amount of the death benefit paid on the death of the insured. Any outstanding loan on a policy, no matter how it has been described or computed, is deducted from the benefits payable to the survivor and so, Mr. Speaker, at some time along the way the loans are repaid.
All of us here know that the minister did not prepare this bill, or budget, whichever it is. It was prepared by high-priced mandarins in the Department of Finance. I do not expect a $50,000 or $60,000 a year mandarin to have any feelings for the plight of the lowly wage earner. The value and worth of those mandarins to the government is to find new sources of revenue for the hungry boss. When they come up with a new gimmick, they get a pat on the head and a longer lease on their cushy jobs. The Minister of Finance, on the other hand, is- like myself-an elected representative of the people. The minister's riding is very much like my own, comprised largely of wage earners and farmers, and it is a long way from being a Rosedale or a Mount Royal. The minister must surely have more feeling for the little man than a mandarin, insulated as he is from the realities of earning a meagre wage or salary.
The minister should never have approved any part of this bill dealing with the taxation of life insurance policies. I know that part of the bill evolved before he was moved to his new portfolio, but all the same he should have deleted this section from the bill presently before us. This whole section dealing with the taxation of insurance policy benefits is shifty, devious and totally unwarranted, and it should be struck from the bill.
I make my recommendation as a result of over 100 letters that I have received from constituents.
I should like to turn to the provisions for tax rebates outlined in this bill. Here, again, there is an obvious effort on the part of the government to deceive. There is no clearcut policy in this section that spells out the manner in which the rebate will be effected. The minister proposes to put the onus on employers to give the rebate to employees. It is not a directive, but is more in the way of a request. It is rather like saying to the employer that it would be very nice if some way
November 17, 1977

could be found to give each employee the $100 rebate, which amounts to less than $2 per week and which is not very much.
Without specific direction on the manner in which the rebate will be made, it could, and probably will, be paid in dribs and drabs-not in a lump sum which would have the most desirable effect on our public economy and the economy of the recipient. The only way such a rebate would have a stimulating effect on the economy, especially such a small amount as $100, would be for taxpayers to receive the money in a lump sum. It is very likely that having an extra $100 which is not committed to a specific purpose, such as paying the rent or making a car payment, would encourage people to make purchases that have been delayed. 1 am thinking of hard goods such as refrigerators, stoves and other appliances of the larger and more expensive type.
This would help to wipe out the inventories of appliances that exist throughout the country, and stimulate new production. I do not believe spending by individuals of $100 or $200 on necessities, or even luxuries, would have very much effect on the level of inflation. I cannot accept the proposal of the Minister of Finance to defer the tax rebate until next year. If we approve the rebate, let us make it effective with the 1977 taxation year and let us decide ourselves how it will be accomplished. Leaving it to employers would result in the money being dribbled out piecemeal in scores of different ways, and it would be highly improper.
It is not the proper function of the private sector to engage in the distribution, allocation or in any other type of management of tax moneys. The only way in which the private sector can engage in the management of taxes is to collect taxes in the name of the Crown. It is for ourselves, the elected representatives of the people, to decide how tax moneys are to be distributed and allocated.
Another section of this bill which troubles me is the one dealing with changes in the rules affecting the operation of the registered home ownership saving plans. The government has resorted to overkill in an attempt to close off a few loopholes in the original program. Tens of thousands of Canadians have invested in the registered home ownership savings plan since 1974 in the honest belief that it would be an ongoing program. There is no reason why it should not continue to be an ongoing program with firm rules and guidelines.
In the two-year period of 1974-1975, 597,000 Canadians invested a total of $564 million in the home ownership savings plan. Seventy-four per cent of those people had annual incomes of less than $15,000. They invested in registered home ownership savings plans under a set of rules that had been established and approved by the federal government. Granted, we in the official opposition warned in 1974, and on subsequent occasions, that there were loopholes in that legislation and that the way had been left open for certain types of abuses. But our warnings and advice were ignored. The government mandarins have discovered a way to put the tax bite on all holders of registered home ownership savings plans, simply by changing the rules. These are drastic changes, and
Income Tax
thousands of innocent and honest Canadians are liable to be caught in the squeeze.
This is criminally deceptive, and I would venture to guess that the Department of Finance mandarins have already computed to the dollar how much additional tax revenue the government will be able to squeeze out of these unsuspecting investors. There is no doubt in my mind that this is a budget we are debating. All it needs is for the Minister of Finance to admit he wanted to table a budget, but wanted at the same time to avoid the responsibility of bringing in a budget with some meaning.
There are no real cures in this budget for any of the pressing economic problems we are facing today. Most of the provisions in this bill are mere window-dressing for the central purpose of the document, and that is, to extend the government's risky, flimsy line of credit. I hope it will not be necessary for the government to call the International Monetary Fund into our financial problem before the spring, but it could happen. I am not fooled by it; I am appalled and disgusted.
I should like to make a few remarks on the procedure introduced by the government to increase its borrowing authority, the main purpose of which is purported to be to amend the Income Tax Act. On page 646 of Hansard for November 7, 1977, the Minister of Finance is reported as saying:
The government intends to introduce a bill soon providing a new procedure which will give ample opportunity for normal debate. In the meantime, there is need for an increase in the borrowing authority.
The minister was referring to his earlier remarks recorded on the same page when he stated that the Financial Administration Act provides that no money shall be borrowed or security issued by or on behalf of Her Majesty without the authority of parliament. That is pretty straightforward. I do not think there has ever been any doubt on the part of members of this House as to what that means. The minister's alleged concern that this House should have ample opportunity to debate a government request for borrowing authority is specious. We are debating such a request at the present time although it is neither the proper time nor the proper vehicle for such a debate. More than one hon. member of this House has brought this point to Your Honour's attention prior to my doing so. We are debating a bill that seeks to accomplish a matter that should properly be debated as a separate issue, not in the context of amending the Income Tax Act.
We are, in effect, telling the Minister of Finance and the government that they are off base. I have to wonder if the minister hoped we would overlook the fact that he had slipped the request for a $9 billion extension of the government's line of credit into this bill, or if he expected us to just treat it as casually as he seems to treat it.
I would like to throw in an aside at this point, Mr. Speaker, based on a press release circulated a couple of days ago by the Canadian International Development Agency. That agency has just granted long-term loans, no doubt at a very low rate of interest, totalling $20 million to the African country of Zaire.

November 17, 1977
Income Tax
In addition, CIDA is throwing in an outright gift to that country of $7 Vi million. This money is intended to assist Zaire to develop its forest industry. The press release noted that Zaire is one of the Francophone countries.
The Canadian forest industry is one of the largest employers in some of our provinces, notably British Columbia, and that industry is in serious difficulty. The Canadian forest industry is presently laying off workers and the immediate and future prospects of that industry are anything but bright. This loan and grant to Zaire reminds me of the CIDA loan to Cuba a few years ago, a matter that 1 brought to the attention of this House. Originally, CIDA had offered Cuba an interest-free loan of $10 million in addition to some millions in outright grants. I objected to this practice and the very modest interest rate of 3 per cent which was applied to the Cuban loan.
The then minister of finance, Mr. Turner, was questioned in the House more than once on this matter. I questioned him. He managed to put on a ridiculously low interest rate of 3 per cent. That is what the government is doing with our money. As the hon. member said, it was done so that Cuba could send troops to Angola. That is what this government does with the taxpayers' money. That is why it is in the worst financial position of any government since the first one in 1867.
We are debating the question of raising more taxes and giving the government authority to borrow an additional $9 billion. I insist that that money should be spent on programs and projects that will further the interests of Canadians first, the lumber industry in British Columbia for example, and if there is any left we can then decide who else in the world is entitled to the money raised by taxing Canadian citizens.
Canada is in a bad position. Yesterday I noted an article by the eminent writer and publisher, Richard S. Malone, in the Globe and Mail. I quote from that article:
Scandals, kickbacks, wiretaps-Almost since its inception the Trudeau government has been guilty of shabby behaviour.
Each week in Ottawa as more charges are made of waste, scandal and cover-ups, the conviction grows that our nation despite all its advantages of wealth and social advancement has lost direction and is sick with an ancient disease. The symptoms are inflation, unemployment, disunity, a falling dollar, enormous debts and public apathy.
Other countries throughout history have suffered from a similar sickness.
Some have never recovered. Malone goes on to state the serious symptoms of this dilemma which faces us. I quote:
We are still in the grip of serious inflation. We spend recklessly and borrow mindlessly committing our children to a debt for years to come.
That is timely. Here the government is asking for $9 billion to pay interest on interest.
We price ourselves out of world markets and pay the penalty of high unemployment, again at the expense of our youth.
We buy the dream of having the highest wage rates in the world by printing more dollars, issuing more bonds and borrowing more money abroad.
We crowd to our airports complaining of hard times as we make our way to Hawaii or California, piling up a tourist deficit of more than a billion dollars and promising to double it next time around.
We accept a budget deficit this year that will be greater than our entire budget was less than ten years ago.
We countenance rates of crime, drug addiction, child abuse, violence and sexual perversion that soar to staggering levels.
We endure scandals in public affairs that make headlines every week.
That is all I want to quote from Mr. Malone. I am sure all members will agree with that article, regardless of their political leanings. I add to that one short sentence: a scandal a day is the Liberal way. There is one more point I would like to make before I conclude. I draw the attention of the House to still another breach of faith on the part of this government. Earlier this year the government sought the help of Canadians to reduce the waste of energy, specifically to insulate their homes and thereby reduce the consumption of home heating oil. The government offered grants of up to $350 toward the cost of insulation. I compliment them on that policy. I agree with it. Many of my constituents have taken advantage of it. Some failed to do so after receiving the particulars. After the program was well under way we found that the grants have to be added to a person's income for tax purposes. It is just a little thing, perhaps, but it does add another straw to the camel's back. I do not think those grants should be taxable.
I wish to conclude my remarks by saying a few words about the national or public debt. I asked the Minister of Finance to enlighten us on that score, but so far I have not heard from the minister or his parliamentary secretary. I received some information since then which I will relate to the House. As of March 31 this year, the gross national debt stood at $67,075 million. Inasmuch as the present request for $9 billion in additional borrowing authority is in addition to the new tax revenue sought in this same bill, we can assume that the gross national debt for the coming year will reach or even exceed $75 billion. Interest paid this year on the national debt was $5,350 million, or 13 per cent of our total national budget. As of March 31 of this year, Canada's net recorded assets totalled $37.5 billion. This means we have a net national debt of $29.5 billion. To sum it up, we owe $29.5 billion more than we are worth. Mr. Speaker, no business of any kind could survive under those conditions.
When the Prime Minister came to power nine years ago, the gross national debt amounted to $39.2 billion, part of which was due to the financing of two world wars and two lesser wars. In just nine years of Trudeaucracy, as someone termed it, the spending policies of the government have increased the national debt more than 100 per cent. Added to this is the fact that we now have a 90-cent dollar. We are in a hole there, too. For every cent by which the Canadian dollar is depressed, the country loses $60 million a year on the basis of our present adverse trade balance. Thus, if our trade balance position does not improve-and there is not much encouragement to believe it will-it is going to cost us $600 million a year to keep this country solvent. That is the result of nine years of Trudeaucracy under this Socialist-Liberal government which the Canadian people have had to endure.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot, in all conscience, support any part of the bill before us. I would support the tax cuts to our citizens if they were meaningful and if I knew how the tax cuts and

November 17, 1977

rebates were going to be accomplished. But I cannot support the government's request for an increase of $9 billion in borrowing authority. I strongly urge that the provision to this effect be removed from the bill, after which the minister might bring it before us again in a proper manner so that the elected representatives of the people could deal with it.
Mir. Cyril Symes (Sault Ste. Marie): Mr. Speaker, we have before us a bill which is of extreme importance to the Canadian people. It is important for what it does to them as well as for them. I should like, in the course of my remarks, to draw attention to areas in which I think the budget bill is inadequate, and to propose some alternative ideas for the consideration of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in the hope that when we get to committee of the whole we might prevail upon the government to bring forth some meaningful amendments.
When the opposition comments on bills brought before the House, we often hear from the Liberal benches that we are negative, that we are preaching gloom and doom and that everything, really, is pretty good in the context of the world situation. We are told that Canadian problems are not of our own making, but that somehow they are the result of world economic conditions which we are unable to change. I do not accept that kind of philosophy because, surely, a government, by virtue of its economic, taxation, employment and trade policies, plays a highly significant part in determining a nation's affairs. It is precisely because I am concerned about the sad state of our economy that I wish to criticize the measures we see before us in this bill and other measures put forward by the government.
I do not accept the argument that Canada is doing well by comparison with other countries, when I find that other industrialized nations, during the period in which the Prime Minister has been in office, have held their unemployment rates to a figure consistently below one-half of Canada's, and when I see that our inflation rate, despite controls, is higher than that of the United States without a control program. But I am most deeply disturbed by the lack of attention on the part of the Minister of Finance to the high degree of unemployment facing the nation. Unemployment is the number one problem, yet somehow I do not think the message has come through to the policymakers on the other side.
Over the past few years we have witnessed a preoccupation with inflation and with policies to control it. Unfortunately, those policies have failed. Inflation is still running at 9 per cent, well above the government's target. At the same time, the anti-inflation program has destroyed our economy to the extent that there is tremendously high unemployment-presently more than one million Canadians, taking into account the hidden unemployment figures. I shall attempt to show that the policies placed before us will not reduce unemployment, as the government says, but will only mean further hardship for millions of Canadians-the unemployed and their families- over the winter months. I want to outline some of my reasons for believing this policy will not work, and propose alternative plans.

Mr. Speaker, I think I have more than two minutes left. I looked up the Hansard for that day, and it was pretty obvious to me that I had not spoken for 18 minutes. I said when I last spoke that we were opposing this bill because what is being suggested here would give a tremendous amount of power to the company to do things it has not been able to do until now. I said that while I thought the company was very good at protecting its officers and its shareholders, it was not very concerned about protecting the users of the telephone service in Ontario and Quebec. I should like to quote from an article reporting a statement by the president of the Public Service Alliance, Mr. Andy Stewart. I quote again, Mr. Speaker, because I want to correct an impression I left. I quote the article as follows:
When the chief executive officer of Bell Canada retired, Stewart said, he received a lump sum payment of $575,000, was made a member of the board of directors at $201,000 a year and was guaranteed a $ 100,000-a-year pension when he fully retired.
Mr. Speaker, I was able to get access, and I am not suggesting for a moment that it is difficult to get access, to a page from the annual report of Bell Canada for 1976. This page deals with remuneration, direct remuneration and the estimated annual benefits upon retirement of senior Bell Canada officials. I would like to quote from a page of the annual report of Bell Canada for 1976. I wish, Mr. Speaker, that we had the right they have in the United States Congress to put something on the record, because this page is really a table which is much clearer when looked at than when read as Hansard will report it. The page has three columns, with three

(January 1 to April 30) chairman of the board and chief executive officer of Bell Canada: director of NTL. (May 2 to December 31) chairman of the board and chief executive officer of NTL: director of Bell Canada, Nedco, NTL.

Includes Bell Canada's contributions under the employees' savings plan (1970). In addition to such remuneration, eligible officers who are enrolled in Bell Canada's employees' savings plan, as in effect from July I. 1966, to June 30, 1970, are entitled to-

speechtext:
I am interested, Mr. Speaker, in the application that Bell Canada has under Bill C-1001 for a change in their financing structure. I am actually more interested in the reasons they are before us today. Everyone, I am sure, is in agreement that Bell is a multinational corporation, probably controlled by Bell of the United States and probably has more than a working agreement with IT and T, the largest multinational corporation in the world. They work very closely with each other in the manufacturing of goods in their subsidiary companies, and their purchasing structures, and in fact are probably the largest public monopoly in the world-their public monopoly, not in ownership but in the service that they are supposed to, and anticipate they do, render.
Bell Canada and, in fact, any public utility of that nature is very important to the nation. They are so important that when we set up our structure in Canada it was mandatory that agencies such as public utilities, whether they were privately owned or publicly owned, would have to come before parliament for changes in their financial structure, and this applied to only a limited number of things. It applied to railways, it applied to gas and oil pipelines, it applied to insurance companies, trust companies, finance companies, banks and other closely related public agencies. Why were they brought before parliament for changes in their financial structure? One of the reasons is that the public obviously has to be protected against a monopoly. When you grant a monopoly, whether it is for a sewage system, for lights, for streets or for anything that is universally supplied on a monopoly basis, there must be some way of controlling the cost of that service.
In most cases we control these services by having people elected who report to the public and are responsible to the public, both for their election and for their remuneration. In

this case, where we are dealing with a private monopoly corporation in a public utility field, it was always agreed they would have to come to the public before they could change their financial operation and before they were allowed to make expenditures in a totally different field. Over the years some changes have been made. We have now reached the stage where many of these public agencies that were considered of such importance to the public have had to come before parliament to change their certification. They have had to come to change their financial structure. They have had to come to make major changes in the role they are playing in the field in which the federal government has a great deal of interest.
Over the years we have established, by letters patent, changes which have allowed insurance companies to be certified, to make changes in their financial structure, to amalgamate, to join with other companies, to do a number of things. We retained something for ourselves, something that was really no control at all, which was the right to demand in this House that before an order in council was granted allowing the acceptance of those letters patent, we as members of parliament would be able to question the decision the minister was making by order in council.
This type of operation has not worked. For a long time the government has depended on its members to vote for the government, whether or not they knew anything about the subject, whether they were concerned about the subject or, in fact, without any knowledge of the subject at all. So that after the debate was over they could always count on the order in council being approved, because if the members did not approve it there would probably be an election, and most of them were not too interested in having an election over something they did not understand in the first place.
There really has not been any control. Most people do not care if one insurance company has an arrangement or develops an arrangement with another insurance company. So we gave up our rights with the insurance companies. It got to the stage where nobody was too sure what was happening with the pipelines, so we gave that up. We have given up most of the powers for the establishment of public corporations. We have over the last four or five years made changes to the Bank Act which allow us to get rid of the power of parliament, to decide on the extension, capitalization and methods of operation of our national banks. We have really made a lot of concessions in this House, in the interest, I suppose, of getting things done. It seems to me that the public is very interested in some of the agencies over which we no longer have any control.
I am sure that if we were to give passage to Bill C-1001, we would be accomplishing what Bell wants, but we certainly would not be doing very much for the Canadian public. Because it is in a monopoly position in respect of a public utility, Bell really has a licence to print money. This company has a number of ways of raising money. During a previous debate an hon. member was talking about the national debt being something like $67 billion.

1 think he said $67 billion, but we could bring it up to that level easily by adding Bell's debt which 1 understand is about $2.5 billion. It really would not make much difference. What does Bell really want? It wants to expand into international markets and into other fields than the telephone business, and it wants to do this without any control. It is true that the company has to go before the CTC. Is it the CTC now, or has that been changed?

I guess they got tired of the CTC. They kicked them pretty hard for some time until Bell became experts in dealing with them, so the government changed it to the CRTC and it is now trying to develop experts to handle this monster. Bell is probably doing a little better with the CRTC than it did with the CTC. I am not prepared to let the cabinet deal with this matter. That would really be giving up the right of hon. members to protect the public from this utility. There is absolutely no legitimate reason for a public utility in a monopoly position being privately owned. There is no logical or justifiable reason for that. I can think of no case at all where there has been a public utility owned by the people, turned over to the private sector after being operated as a public utility.
Perhaps 1 should say that I can think of one instance. I know of a number of corporations which got rid of their garbage collection systems and turned them over to private enterprise. In most cases the cost went up and up to the point that the municipalities or corporations had to take the operations back and run the garbage collection system again. I do not know of any municipalities which have turned their lighting companies over to private enterprise, and I do not know of any that have turned sidewalk construction or road building and maintenance over to private enterprise. I can remember they started out that way in Montreal and one had to pay to cross the bridge until everybody, even those in the province of Quebec, decided they had paid for the bridge time and time again and they wanted to own the bloody thing, so they gave it back to the people.
Generally speaking, I do not think that once a public utility has been owned and operated by the people it is ever transferred the other way. I do not think that even in British Columbia, where all the parties got together under the banner of free enterprise, they turned the hydro company or the roads or other public utilities over to private enterprise. Public utilities enjoy a monopoly position, and they must be in that position, but they certainly should not be in that position for
Bell Canada
the purpose of printing money. That is really the privilege that Bell Telephone is seeking.
I am amazed at the concessions that Bell Canada has been granted. When a hydro company puts power into your house, you get a bunch of connections on the wall. Hydro approves them, and that is the end of it. If you want to put a Westing-house stove in and connect it to hydro, that is fine. If you want to put a Frigidaire in, that is fine. I am sure that General Electric has some equipment in almost every home. The telephone company, on the other hand, says it wants to put in not only the service or the facility, in a monopoly position, but it wants to sell all the parts or appliances to be used on that system: you cannot put in any other make.
The government has got a facility in my house. I hope someone makes up his mind pretty soon whether it is to be changed, because I am sure this company is not going to charge me for it. I am quite prepared to pay the telephone company to come into my house with the service, but that is the end of it. If I want to buy my telephones from Radio Shack, I will do so, and if the company wants to take me to court, that's fine. If I want to rent a telephone from them, that is fine; but if I want to buy one from somebody else, 1 intend to use that one too. As long as it has an acceptable standard stamp on it, then as far as I am concerned it is none of the company's business what I do in my house.
We have given all these concessions to Bell Canada. It now wants the right to increase capitalization without supervision by parliament. This company really does not want to increase its capitalization. What it wants is to be able to do anything it wishes, including increasing capitalization. If the company had just wanted to increase its capitalization, it would have brought a bill before us that said so. I can remember the company coming here when it wanted to increase its board of directors. Did it really make a huge difference to Bell whether it had 15 or 20 directors? It sure made a lot of difference to them when we included an amendment which said that one of those directors had to be appointed by parliament or the government to represent the public, without involving share capital. We were not going to buy the position; we were just going to control one directorship. Let me tell you that they put up a battle for a couple of years over that.
I had very interesting conversations every Friday afternoon with the president of Bell Canada who came to tell us why they could not accept that one directorship. His argument was that we did not need a director on the board to look after subscribers' problems, because he handled all the complaints as president of Bell Telephone.

So no matter what we may think are the merits of the bill-
I do not happen to think the bill has much merit-surely, as members of parliament, we could agree on one principle, namely, that when bills come in front of the House which mean that the House does not have to review them or look at them any more, whether or not we agree with the principle of the bill as designed, we can surely agree on the principle that this is the place to review bills for capitalization change in major corporations.
As I see the bill, it attempts to do a number of things. First, it is a revision of the act of incorporation relating to the company's ability and methodology, including the removal of the scrutiny of the appropriate government regulatory body. It grants Bell, if passed, the power to borrow, issue stock, bonds, debentures or other securities the company deems necessary, plus it would give Bell the right to fix whatever price on the sales that it wished. Subsequent sections would provide Bell with the authority to establish voting rights, by-laws, procedures and alterations to issue shares as Bell may deem necessary. Let me just say, for the record, that I want to know whether an increase in the capitalization will mean that the return on the investment on which the regulatory agency has to pass judgment will have to be increased when you increase the capital structure of the company. 1 would like to have the question clarified as to whether you can increase the invested capital of your company through changing the capital structure under the bill, thereby increasing the rate of return, which is not related to the service that is being provided to the public. In any event, if I am wrong, I would be happy to be corrected on that point, but it seems to me to be a real risk.
In essence, the major criticism continues to be that this bill will have the effect of avoiding the consequences of a parliamentary debate and of avoiding the consequences of MPs scrutinizing that company. In effect, it will take away from us, as members of parliament, our sworn duty to look after our constituents with regard to these matters. We have heard some public criticism of most telephone companies, some of it by the CRTC. For example, the B.C. Telephone Company has used many beautiful devices for avoiding real regulation. I am relating this matter to the bill because exactly the same principle applies to Bell Canada.
As soon as a telephone monopoly finds any profitability in the company-and I defy anyone to dispute this after examining the record-the first thing that is done is that the profitable section is spun off to make sure that when the regulations come down they regulate only the low profit section, and the
Bell Canada
high profit sections go off into self-owned or partially controlled or owned companies.

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext: Can you give an example?

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) asks for an example. I think probably the best example in B.C. is what happened to certain services provided by B.C. Telephone. Those services used to be under the ambit of B.C. Telephone, and therefore had to be included in terms of the profitability of the company. For years the Canadian Transport Commission regulated the profits of B.C. Telephone and included the most profitable section of the operation, which was its yellow pages and directory service. I do not think it took too long for the company's solicitors and accountants to have a look at this and hive off that profitable operation into a private, self-owned and controlled entity. That profitable operation would therefore no longer be controlled by the regulatory body. Therefore, what the public looks at is the bare bones of the telephone system.
The public gets to look at only the worst example, the operations which do not make a lot of money and which have to return on investments about 6 per cent. I believe that is what they are now allowed on invested capital. When profitable sections of companies are hived off-for example, the purchase of telephone services from wholly owned subsidiaries-we are not dealing at arm's length and we are not dealing with the market price.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) talked about rental arrangements. It is almost impossible to buy a telephone. Everything is rented. 1 remember having a little buzzer put into my law office. I think I was charged 50 cents per month for that buzzer. The buzzer was paid for after the first two months. It has now been there about 15 or 16 years, and I feel I own part of the company now. There is a reason why these services are not sold to us. The reason is that in the world of real competition the company would be out of business.
That is the whole basis for our philosophy that a private monopoly does not compete in the free market. Its charges do not compete in the free market, its products do not compete in the free market, and therefore it is an appropriate vehicle for public ownership.

The private monopoly uses its mandate to increase the profitability of its subsidiary companies.
People sometimes accuse us of being against business. I can go through the rates in Canada again, and we will find that the only friend the small businessman has, as far as telephone rates are concerned, is this party, because public telephone rates for business are consistently lower all across the country. I did want to spend a moment or two on a subject which is directly related to the question of the change in telephone company capitalization. It deals with a very abrasive strike in the province of B.C. which has been going on for some time between B.C. Telephone and its workers. The workers in that company have been kicked around in the press. They have had rotating strikes and they have blocked traffic. Mr. Speaker, people are tired of strikes. They see the disruption, but they do not see what is behind the dispute.
Let me tell what happened in the B.C. Telephone Company dispute. A conciliation commission recommended settlement within the AIB guidelines. In other words, the recommendation to the union was to settle below the AIB guidelines, and the union accepted that recommendation. The company, how-

November 17, 1977

ever, has rejected the conciliation report and has attempted to remove the job security clause that the union has had two years. That is what is at the heart of the dispute.
Why is there a dispute? Bell Canada, because of an AIB rollback, had a windfall profit of some $13 million, and I believe B.C. Telephone was looking for exactly the same result in this dispute with its employees. When it did not get it, it found it could carry the stress anyway. If you examine the merits of that dispute objectively you will find that the workers in the union are on the right side of the issue.
That particular dispute could be settled tomorrow, but one of the reasons it is not settled is that this private monopoly does not have to withstand the market forces where people are in competition. A strike or a labour dispute is usually an economic war-how long can the workers hold out, how long can the company hold out? A private monopoly can hold out forever because, at the end of the road, all it has to do is go to the regulatory body and say, "Those are our costs, that is our capitalization, such and such is the rate of return we must have on our investment." That is one of the reasons we will have increasing labour trouble in Canada-private monopoly telephone companies.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this argument we have been hearing from the New Democratic Party on telephone rates. There are a few things with which they are not acquainted. There are no low telephone rates in large cities like New York, Los Angeles, Toronto or Montreal. Hon. members of that party might be under the impression that volume leads to low rates. Large cities do not have low telephone rates however, because it is very costly for the telephone company to provide trunking facilities, exchange facilities and so on.
Members of the New Democratic Party have mentioned the efficiency of provincial telephone companies which are Crown
Bell Canada
corporations. I worked for one of them for 30 years, Mr. Speaker, and I know that today they are run on advice and specifications provided by Bell Telephone. They are called Bell specifications. The telephone companies of Alberta, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan get these specifications from Bell and Northern on how to run the commercial department, the plant department, and the engineering department. These are provinces with small populations, and low rates can be provided in cities like Winnipeg, Brandon, Saskatoon, Regina, and even Edmonton.
In large centres, especially Ontario, it is very costly to provide exchange and trunking facilities. In areas like Mississauga it costs hundreds of millions of dollars to provide telephone service. Everytime a new centre is built with a population of 100,000 or so, it must have access to all other parts of greater Toronto and Ontario. This is very costly and it is why the rates are high. That is the difference between the Crown corporations in the small provinces and Bell. I must emphasize again that they get all their information on how to operate from Bell and Northern.
I hope I have made that clear to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). I did not have a chance to speak on that point the other day.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this adjournment debate I should like to refer to my question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) on November 14 in which I tried to explain the weaknesses which exist in the Canadian home insulation program. The program denies the persons in Canada who need it most the advantage of the grants which are paid.
As I have pointed out before, there has been a program in existence which provides what is needed for those people on fixed and low incomes, who cannot afford the increases in fuel oil or in hydro power, in order for them to cope with the cost of living which exists today. On a number of occasions I have brought this to the attention of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). It is one of the best programs ever produced by the government. I refer to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. It provides everything that a person on low income needs, but cannot afford, in order to have that insulation.
There are many homeowners in Newfoundland with fixed or low incomes in the $6,000 or lower category. Their homes are deteriorating because they cannot afford to maintain them with the present cost of building materials. How can they take advantage of this $350 grant when they do not have a porch, verandah, walls or windows that keep out the cold; storm windows, proper plumbing, basement, a proper heating system or proper electric wiring? That program, which has been in existence for four years, provides grants of up to $3,750 to allow them to do that. It provides grants of up to $750 for those in the $10,000 bracket.
Granted, the home insulation program will fill a need for some people. However, it eliminates those who need to save fuel the most because they cannot afford it.
Every time I have questioned this in the past two or three years, I have been told there is not enough money available. However, the government now comes out with a massive $1.4 billion program, the Canadian Home Insulation Program. This is contradictory to its other programs and is directed to only a few people.
I do not know how these programs are devised. It is so ridiculous it is not even funny. What they do is set up a new bureaucracy. I can see their hands moving now. With the $1.4 billion, they can build a new bureaucracy and promote some people.
One office was set up in Montreal to handle the 1.2 million people who will qualify in the first year. There is only one number that these people can call. The people in my district cannot get through to Montreal. They cannot even get through to me because of lack of telephone service. What about those in the Yukon or Northwest Territories?
The government has come out with this $1.4 billion program. However, in the first year it is providing only $45
Adjournment Debate
million to satisfy 133,000 units. The minister stated that there have been 60,000 applications. That was in only two months since the program started September 1. If every application were approved, it would take $30 million. Therefore, how are they providing any help?
There is something else I cannot understand. Through this program members of the government are creating discrimination and destroying national unity. The country has been divided into different regions under this program. In Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island the citizens there receive $350 for $350 spent. God bless them, they need it. However, in other provinces you must spend $500 to receive $350. I do not see the reasoning.
This country has also been separated because in New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan, only homes built prior to 1921 can qualify. Dwellings in Newfoundland, Alberta, British Columbia and the Territories qualify if they were built prior to 1941. It amazes me how they can keep confusing the people.

NATIONAL HARBOURS BOARD-SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT ACTING IN ANTICIPATION OF PASSAGE OF BILL C-6
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this session of parliament we should be hearing a great deal about ports, more especially when Bill C-6 comes up for debate and when the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) and I try to unravel the somewhat curious hesitancy of the Ministry of Transport in trying to question whether there should be an increase in containerization in Halifax, though certainly there has been rather indecent haste about providing for Montreal although, as far as I can see, the needs of both are about equal. But my main purpose this evening is to concentrate on Bill C-6 and, if I can, obtain some reassurance from the ministry about the future of the 150 or so people who work for the National Harbours Board and for the ports and harbours division of the Ministry of Transport. These people are very much affected by Bill C-6 which would replace much of the existing administration of our harbours across Canada with arrangements which are very, very new.
My understanding is that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is legally quite entitled to go ahead and have the officials in his department prepare for the day when the provisions of Bill C-6 become law, so that the administrative structure would be in readiness. But that is as far as it goes. Until the bill becomes the law of the land he may not start that administrative apparatus going. This is as it should be, after all.
The Department of Transport, at least the chairman and others of the National Harbours Board, and I have the Chair-

man's memorandum here before me, Mr. Pierre A. H. Fran-che, have acted with some dispatch in this matter but not exactly to the liking of a large number of employees who are now, frankly, I think scared to death, it may be that the minister's representative when he speaks will be able to quieten their fears, but their fears are in two particular areas. First, they were promised that any hiring in the future ports structure would have equal representation from both the Department of Transport and the National Harbours Board. We are told that this is not so, that it is only the Board which will have the say in the hiring, and the people in the Department of Transport-that is the section of that ministry I have referred to-are pretty uptight, and I would hope that the minister's representative would be able to set their fears at rest on this matter.
Secondly, those who are passing through the screening process were assured that the process of bilingualism would not substantially change the numbers now involved in the operations of Canadian ports. Our understanding, and again the minister's representative might be able to set the record very precisely on this point, is that of the 150 jobs in the new port set-up, 135 are to be classified as bilingual. This raises the very substantial question: by what criteria has the figure of 135 been reached, and why is it substantially in excess of the numbers who are now classified as bilingual?
I do not quarrel with the principle of bilingualism as such, but when you look at the numbers of ports across Canada, one would have to think of places such as Vancouver, and to a lesser extent Halifax, Saint John, St. John's, Newfoundland, Hamilton, and all of the other ports within the jurisdiction of the former or outgoing National Harbours Board, now to be within this new empire, and wonder whether as high as 135 of 150 is a necessary Figure. Perhaps we can have an answer to that.
Again, I admit there is a justification for government, for this particular department and the minister to start reorganization now, but there comes a point at which they must take into account the House of Commons, the other place, and the Governor General who all have their say in this whole process, that is, there has to be a parliamentary enactment giving a blessing to this change that will be brought about by Bill C-6.
Mr. Franche in his letter to employees had this to say, and I will quote one paragraph from it. The letter is available to anyone who may wish to see it.
Since the Minister of Transport has tasked-
That is a bureaucratic word "tasked".
-the Commissioner-Designate with the responsibility of having an operational organization in place when the Canada Ports Act is promulgated, we must begin now to co-ordinate all the activities concerned with ports administration in Canada.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-APPLICABILITY OF GUIDELINES TO AWARDING OF MEDAL TO PREMIER LEVESQUE BY FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I participate in this debate this evening as a result of a question asked by my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie), and also of my own question of yesterday addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), which was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Car the minister tell the House if the medal awarded to Premier Levesque by the Government of France, which I understand is the second highest award that can be given by the French government, fell within the 1968 guidelines issued by the Government of Canada governing the receipt of medals and honours by Canadian nationals?
The minister, in effect, refused to answer my question when he said in reply that, first of all, the guidelines had no legal effect and were in no way binding upon anybody. I think that is a terrible admission to be made by a minister of a government which has issued some rather strict sounding guidelines.
Secondly, he said that the medal was widely distributed and therefore did not carry much distinction, so he did not even consider it necessary to check those guidelines. I think it is interesting to check the facts in this regard. This is a very old award in the history of France.
As I understand it, the Legion of Honour was established by Emperor Napoleon in 1807 or thereabouts. It is instructive to note that the first recipient of this honour was Czar Alexander of Russia. Some five years later Russia was invaded by the French. I do not know if that has any bearing on whether Mr. Levesque feels any insecurity as a result of the medal being awarded to him recently. However, the guidelines are clear that approval is not given to accept an order or decoration which is in relation to events more than five years prior to the proposal for the award.
I do not know whether Mr. Levesque received this award for services as a war correspondent during the Second World War. That was not stated. Being employed by the U.S. government, I suppose he did not feel it necessary to help Canada in that war effort.
The award is not approved for anyone who receives it on the basis of something which is at variance with considerations of general policy or public interest. I do not know what Mr. Levesque has done lately in this country which is good for the general policy or public interest of Canadians who wish to maintain our federation.
Section 3 of the guidelines says the following:
Approval is, otherwise, contemplated in the case of any Canadian citizen ... to whom an honour or decoration is offered on one of the following grounds:
(a) for an extraordinary service to mankind;
I will be happy to hear from the parliamentary secretary whether Mr. Levesque has performed an extraordinary service to mankind or, as set out in subsection (b), has shown conspicuous bravery in saving or attempting to save life. Subsection (c) refers to important and personal services rendered to the

Subsection (d) refers to services rendered while in the salaried employment of the donor country. That may be interesting. Approval is also contemplated when there is recognition of an exceptional achievement or service.
The minister said that this is a widely distributed medal. It is interesting to note that only one other Canadian prior to Mr. Levesque received this award. That was Ambassador Roy, who was Canadian ambassador to France for more than 25 years. That is a significant achievement, but that shows the importance the French place on distributing this award. I suppose "widely distributed" means that if it is awarded once it has wide distribution. It is interesting to note the effect of distribution on these guidelines. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the debate on this budget bill was interrupted for private members' hour, I was outlining my concerns about the inadequacies of the budget introduced last March and subsequently reaffirmed a couple of weeks ago by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).
Canada's number one problem is unemployment, but I do not see that recognition in the budget before us. On other occasions I have gone into the reasons why we have high unemployment in this country: the dependence on resource based industries, the lack of manufacturing, and the lack of research and development to stimulate our manufacturing industry. I will not belabour that point at the moment.
November 17, 1977

As all members are aware, the unemployed and their families are the first to experience the pain and dislocation which come with not having a job. I wonder how many working Canadians understand what they themselves pay in terms of this high unemployment? We are experiencing the effects of approximately one million jobless Canadians. We all have to recognize what is happening to our unemployment insurance program.
For the first half of 1977 payouts in the unemployment insurance program totalled $2.1 billion; but the projections are that by the end of this winter the total cost of this program will have doubled to $4 billion in order to keep people off the welfare rolls. The fund does not have enough money to make that kind of payout, and therefore working Canadians have to pay for this high unemployment through their tax dollars in supplementing the unemployment insurance fund.
Also because of high unemployment, we suffer from the loss of billions of dollars in tax revenue. The government does not get tax revenue from Canadians who are unemployed. That means there is less room to manoeuvre to maintain programs such as the old age pension. I wonder if every working Canadian realizes that last year every man, woman, and child lost approximately $520 in goods and services not produced because of high unemployment. Family problems, alcoholism, marital break-up, and increased crime are caused partially by the high unemployment we are experiencing today.
One of the saddest repercussions is the disillusionment which this causes to young people, whether they be university, community college, or high school graduates out on the labour market for the first time. We have told our young people to get an education and the world would be theirs. Unfortunately today we find 46 per cent of the unemployed in this country are under 35 years of age. Even after having high hopes and training, the young people are the first not to find a job. I worry about what is happening to the future generation of workers whom we are going to depend on when they experience this kind of disillusionment because the country has not organized its economy in such a way to give them that all-important job. I think of the most disillusioning experience I saw first-hand.
I travelled with the leader of our party a few months ago to Newfoundland. We looked at the state of the unemployed there. That is not unemployment that is seasonal, but unemployment that has affected adults and young people year after year. No matter how hard they try, the job vacancies are not there.
A kind of dependent psychology is beginning to take hold in areas of Atlantic Canada where there is no hope of ever finding a permanent job. This was vividly demonstrated to me in a little slip of the phrase, I suppose, when we were interviewing some unemployed people. We were talking about unemployment insurance payouts. They never referred to it as we do, as an insurance program. They called it "the pension . Unemployment had become a way of life, and unemployment
Income Tax
insurance had become their only means of livelihood. Therefore they looked upon it as a pension. They were dependent on it. The whole idea of the work ethic had been eroded through no fault of their own, but through the fault of the Canadian and provincial governments which had so organized the economy that these people could not find work.
I am also concerned about the government's analysis of those who are unemployed. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) has often said that unemployment is not all that serious because so many of the unemployed are women and young people. They are looked upon as secondary earners, people who are really not that serious about seeking a job or for whom having a job is not as important as the so-called breadwinner, the adult male of the family.
Let us look at that argument and the statistics we have for last year on the unemployed. They are the latest available. I am indebted to H. L. Robinson, an economist, who has written in the September issue of Canadian Forum a brilliant analysis of this problem.
When we look at this 1.1 million unemployed Canadians, how does it break down? We find that unemployed men represent about 8.9 per cent of the labour force. Breaking that sector down into age groups, those 15 to 24 years old represent 17.7 per cent of the labour force, and those over 25 years old, 6.1 per cent.
When we look at the women who are unemployed, we find that they represent not 8.9 per cent but 14.5 per cent of the unemployed. With the age groups, those 15 to 24 years old represent 18.1 per cent, and those over 25, 12.8 per cent. In other words, the majority of the unemployed in this country today are young people or women. The majority of these unemployed belong to families in which at least one other person is working.
Given those statistics, the Minister of Employment and Immigration advances the argument that somehow unemployment among this group of women and young people really is not that serious. Because they are not adult males, the breadwinner of the family, their unemployment is only secondary.
Aside from the male chauvinism in that argument, the minister and his colleagues ignore a very important fact, the fact that so many wives and young men and women work for the following reasons. First, they have to work in order to supplement the family income so that they can make ends meet. With the kind of inflation that we have, one income is simply not enough to maintain or improve the standard of living in relation to the inflation of the past few years. What do I have to back up that contention?
Using figures from 1975, the latest available, we find that the average annual wage earnings in Canada were $10,574. That is what the average person earned in 1975. The average family income in the same year was $13,805. If you look at the breakdown of those earnings, you find that 60 per cent of all wage earners had incomes below the average of $10,574.
According to Statistics Canada, any family with an income in an urban centre of $8,422 or below was classified at the

November 17, 1977
Income Tax
poverty level. When 60 per cent of the workers are earning less than the average wage and the poverty line is only about $2,000 below the average wage, you begin to appreciate why so many wives and young people have to work to supplement the family income.
Is it any wonder that family members other than the adult male, the traditional breadwinner, have to find jobs to help pay the bills? Women and young people are in the labour force out of economic necessity. They are not "secondary" workers in terms of the needs of the majority of Canadian families today.
I also want to say to the Minister of Employment and his officials that the women and young people are not secondary in the work force today because the nature of the jobs in our work force has changed. The service sector of our economy has grown tremendously. Nursing, social services, hotels, restaurants, secretarial, clerking, teaching and other such services have grown. In 1956 only 48.5 per cent of jobs in Canada were in the service industry. In 1976 that had increased to 65.5 per cent.
If you claim that these people are only secondary and not serious income earners or serious to the work force, I shudder to think what would happen to our economy and the businesses that employ them if they were removed from the work force. I dare say that members of parliament would not be able to function since their staffs are primarily made up of women and young adults.
Women and young people are essential in our economy on both the supply and demand side. Their unemployment is no less tragic than the unemployment of the traditional unemployed male. These people are not secondary in importance. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says that unemployment is a serious problem, but it is blown all out of proportion. That is a falsehood. We know from his own government department, Statistics Canada, that for every 100 unemployed in Canada today, there are only four vacant full-time jobs.
The unemployed are not lazy. They are not avoiding work. I dare the Prime Minister to go to Sudbury and say that there are jobs just begging for people to take in light of the recent INCO lay-offs. Therefore job creation must be of primary importance in the budget before us. I do not see that.
The government is bringing forward tax policies that I consider to be the wrong ones at the wrong time. It has brought forward a $1.2 billion corporate tax concession. I know my Liberal friends will immediately say we are opposed to any kind of corporate tax concession. That is not true. I want to argue that the kind of tax concessions they are bringing forward at this time are wrong in light of what is happening in our economy.
The other element of the job creation program in the budget is $150 million to supplement existing programs. We say that is not going to work. I will explain that later. We need an emergency job creation program at this time.
The New Democratic Party has outlined how we can create from 250,000 to 300,000 jobs during the winter months. We would give a billion and a half dollars tax cut to low and

middle income taxpayers to stimulate buying power, decrease the present level of unused capacity in the economy, and create an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 jobs. We find support for this suggestion from no less a prestigious group than the Economic Council of Canada composed of businessmen, economists, and others from all walks of life, who also called for a tax cut of more than $2 billion to stimulate employment.
We would not want to cut back on family allowances and old age pensions, as the government has hinted it might do, nor would we want to see continued the plight in which the veterans have been placed because of the government's refusal to increase their pensions to a reasonable level-I am thinking particularly of veterans' disability pensions.
We would also favour the introduction of a $400 million federal-provincial-municipal capital works program, similar to the 1971 job creation program, which would create around 60,000 new jobs. We want to see a $500 million housing and urban transit program capable of creating 70,000 jobs, particularly in the construction industry. We also want to see a $50 million program of assistance to small businesses, currently so hard-pressed, which would assist them in hiring approximately 20,000 new employees, especially young people. These are some of the proposals which we put forward as leading to the creation of jobs on an emergency basis.
There is no need to resort to further deficit financing in order to finance the program I have just outlined. What we would do is this: we would redirect some of the tax policies the government has proposed in the budget. For example, we would end the $1.2 billion in tax concessions to large corporations announced last March and reintroduced by the Minister of Finance, and redirect it to personal income tax cuts. This is not because we say, as if in blinkers, that all corporate tax incentives are wrong. But these concessions are designed to encourage corporations to invest and expand their plants. We say it is a ridiculous policy at the present time because industry is only operating at about 80 per cent of its capacity. What businessman in his right mind would use these tax concessions to expand, when he cannot use his existing production line to full advantage?
Could there be any more ridiculous example of the failure of this policy than the realization that INCO, for example, will have received $10 million as a result of these measures, and has recently announced its intention to lay off 3,500 workers?
Alcan, which has profited from these measures to the extent of $11 million, has laid off 400 workers, and Noranda, to whom the concessions have meant $5 million, has already laid off 500 workers, and there are threats that another 1,200 will be laid off in the Gaspe region. This certainly flies in the face of all the assertions that these concessions generate employment. The fact is, and I use the government's own statistics, that since these budget tax concession measures were introduced last March we have seen lay-offs of more than 34,000 workers in the manufacturing industry. The minister is simply misleading the public when he says these concessions are
November 17, 1977

needed to create jobs. They are the wrong concessions at the wrong time.
In today's Globe and Mail we find a survey made by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce which shows that Canada's 300 largest companies do not expect to increase on average their capital spending in real terms in 1978. In other words, the budget measures are a failure. They are not creating the jobs the minister promised they would.
We could also finance the program I have outlined from savings through keeping people off unemployment insurance and keeping them paying income tax as employed persons. The saving in unemployment insurance claims would amount to about $1 billion, and the increased tax revenue from the newly employed would come to around $250 million. Thus, for our emergency job creation program, we could use the same funds as the government has laid out in the present budget, only they would be redirected.
As Eric Kierans, a former Liberal cabinet mihister has noted on many occasions, the government has treated the 1,000 major corporations in this country in a most: generous way. It has probably treated them better than any in the world. The profits of these corporations increased from $7.7 billion in 1970 to $17.8 billion in 1975, an increase of 131 per cent. At the same time, corporate tax rates declined from 29.6 per cent during that period of record profit increase to 26.6 per cent. The government has always favoured big business as opposed to small, and has allowed the corporate sector to defer payment of income tax to the tune of $10 billion. The 1,000 largest corporations owe the government $9 billion of this $10 billion deferment of taxes.
What we need is some attention paid not only to big business, as has always been the case in the past, but to small business which employs 60 per cent of the working people of this country. I am really angry that the government continues to ignore this major sector of our economy.
I have talked to small businessmen on many occasions. I find that their difficulty lies in raising working capital. The banks laugh off the government's small business loans program; they are not interested in it. The Federal Business Development Bank often applies criteria as strict as or even stricter than those imposed on borrowers by private banks. These sources are of no help to small businessmen who have the enterprise or the know-how, but who cannot find the capital to expand or put their projects into operation.
Businessmen also complain to me, time and time again, about the difficulty of obtaining information and management expertise under the programs the government offers. These programs are more often exercises in public relations than anything of substance. Businessmen need assistance, but I am afraid the government programs put roadblocks in their way rather than help them. There is too much government regulation, as they keep pointing out. They are not able to hire expensive accountants and lawyers to give them advice in these areas. The effects of taxation policies, the problems of cash flow, are very onerous.
