If the Minister of Finance were really interested in job creation he would turn more of his attention to the small business sector in terms of tax concessions and the advice he could make available to them. I lament the state of small business. Bankrupticies are up 30 per cent and almost half these business failures involve small businesses in the retail sector. One of the key factors is reduced demand caused by high unemployment and the government's failure to stimulate demand by introducing tax cuts. We want to get the economy healthy again. We have to get Canadians back to work so that they are purchasing goods which the small businessman can supply.
I know the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister keep bringing forward the argument that the problem with business in Canada is that we are pricing ourselves out of world markets. We are told that we are no longer competitive. The Minister of Finance points to our trade deficit as proof of this, but I would like to remind him that the trade deficit includes goods and service transactions. It includes interest and dividends and profit outflows. We have had an over-all deficit for 13 out of the last 16 years. We should know that that deficit is as a result of service transactions by Canadians purchasing imported foreign goods.
In the merchandise trade sector where Canadian workers are involved, there has been a surplus in 15 of the 16 years, and the reason we have had a decline is that the volume of our sales has dropped because the countries which are our customers have been in a recession. I think it should be remembered the end products trade group, that is, the manufactured goods where we have a high labour component, in that group these exports have continued to grow. In fact last year our manufactured exports increased 15 per cent, and they are continuing to increase this year. So I ask the Minister of Finance, if we are pricing ourselves, our manufactured goods, out of the world market, why is it that the volume of our exports is continuing to grow?
I know that the minister is also putting forward a related argument to the phony one of our non-competitiveness, that wage settlements in Canada are higher than those in the United States, and that this justifies holding Canadian wages down to a 6 per cent increase under the AIB over the next year. That wage comparison, I am afraid, is also a myth. What we are trying to do is compare American wages to Canadian wages, but not taking into account the different variables.
First of all are Canadian wages, as the Prime Minister tries to argue, 7 per cent higher than in the United States? Well, the point is that he fails to recognize the Canadian dollar is worth less than the American dollar, so to make that kind of dollar for dollar wage comparison without taking that into account is misleading when our dollar is worth only 90 cents. The Canadian figures also include public service settlements, whereas the United States figures do not. Canadian figures are calculated on base rates, and the U.S. is on average hourly earnings. About 60 per cent of American workers have cost of

living adjustments, but only 30 per cent of Canadians do. You have to take all those factors into consideration when making comparisons. When you do, as the National City Bank of New York has done, you get some pretty interesting revelations.
In 1976, before the 90 cent dollar, making the comparison for wage compensation, taking into account fringe benefits and everything else, the United States worker was paid $7.91 an hour while his Canadian counterpart was paid only $7.05 an hour, or 12 per cent less than his American counterpart-not 7 per cent more as the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister want us to believe. If you take the 90 cent dollar into consideration, the United States worker today is 25 per cent ahead of his Canadian worker in terms of wage settlements.
As well, the Minister of Finance knows Canadian workers have to pay more in interest rates, energy costs, housing, food, and most consumer goods than does his American counterpart.
I am sad that the Prime Minister still makes the workers of Canada the scapegoats for his government's mismanagement. The Liberals continue to hold wage increases below the cost of living increase, because we know the CPI is almost 9 per cent, but the majority of workers will be held to the 6 per cent increase under the guidelines of the anti-inflation program. I ask you, what justice is there in that?

In the budget before us the minister likes to boast about the individual tax relief that is there. He points out quite correctly that an average family of four people with an income of $15,000, for the tax year 1978 will save $100 by the tax credit method, and another $140 through indexing; a $240 tax saving.
Inflation is running at 9 per cent, and this projection will go on for 1978. It is well above the government's guideline of 4 per cent promised under the anti-inflation program. In addition to that, the AIB controls will be in effect for most working Canadians well into 1978. But the government, of course, in the budget announcement has changed the rules. It says that wage increases will be held to 6 per cent even if inflation is at 9 per cent or more. Therefore what happens to the average family which the minister says is going to get such a tax saving? If the income for that family is $15,000, as I have mentioned, they will see their income decline by $450 over the next year despite the tax relief of $240 in the budget. Because of wage controls that family will end up losing $210 in income next year. Where is the fairness in that kind of budgetary measure?
The NDP, supported by the Economic Council of Canada, has argued that what we need to stimulate the economy and to protect the average Canadian from the effects of inflation is a major personal income tax cut. That will stimulate consumer demand. That will create more jobs in the manufacturing industry which is so desperately in trouble at this time. I say to the minister, his budget contains the wrong kind of tax concessions at the wrong time of our economic history. What we need is some protection for the average worker and his family against inflation, which the government has failed to control.
What we need more is a stimulus to consumer demand, as the Economic Council has recommended, so that we can get Canadians back to work again. Unless the government realizes our major problem is unemployment, which has to be tackled by meaningful budgetary measures, I am afraid that we are in for a very, very hard winter indeed, Mr. Speaker, and that things can only get worse.
I say to my colleagues on the Liberal side of the House that what I have tried to do is present an analysis of the problem, and recommend some concrete alternatives to the present policy. I do so in the spirit of trying to work out the best plan for the unemployed in this country. I think the minister has to recognize, as have so many economists, that his present policies are inadequate to deal with this crucial and pressing problem of unemployment.
I hope that when we move back into committee he will be sympathetic to some of our amendments so we can get Canadians back to work, and get consumers and taxpayers protected against the ravages of inflation and unemployment.

Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset I am very pleased to see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is present, and I thank his colleagues from the Privy Council who are here with him too.
The subjects I intend to speak about tonight are not earthshaking, but are important. They are two in number. The first one is SIN, and the second one is potential. To the uninitiated SIN simply means social insurance number. My memory goes back, as the Minister of Finance's memory goes back, to the year 1964 when the Prime Minister of this country gave a solemn promise on the floor of this House that the social insurance number could not be used for anything beyond social services programs, such as unemployment insurance and the Canada Pension Plan. The Prime Minister of that time was well aware of the fact that the great majority of the Canadian people, and in fact the great majority of all free people, do not like to see this gradual closing in of unneeded controls and regulations on the individual.
Parliament reluctantly accepted the social insurance number system in 1964 on the argument that it would make it possible to operate the Canada Pension Plan and unemployment insurance better. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) brought this up in this debate and quoted the passage out of Hansard in which this pledge was made in 1964. The background was simple. The House leader then, who is not present here tonight, was the hon. member for Cape Breton. The leader of the opposition was pressing him on whether they were going to extend this SIN to other uses. What was concerning the leader of the opposition, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), in particular was the fact that the National Revenue people would seize this device as another weapon in their arsenal to control every drop of water, every drop of blood in this country.

November 17, 1977

In response to this type of questioning by the right hon. member for Prince Albert the then Prime Minister said that certainly SIN would not be imposed for the use of the income tax collectors. That was a pledge made in good faith, and 1 am positive it was the viewpoint of every sitting member of parliament, regardless of whether he was a Liberal, a Conservative, a member of the NDP or a Creditiste, because the great majority-in fact all the members of the House-do not like to see the continual erosion of our civil liberties, step by step, at the increasing pace at which they are being eroded today.
The bill that brought about this unhappy change, this breach of a Prime Minister's word to the people of Canada, was brought forward last February. Under a similar type of bill as we are discussing here today, the government was trying to get through the budget resolutions of the 1976 budget. It was a long bill, and way down at the end of the bill was clause 75, an innocuous clause written in legalistic language designed not to attract the attention of members of parliament on any side. It was sneaked into the bill. It had nothing to do with the budget resolutions.
Where were the members of the legislative committee of the cabinet? How did they let that clause slip into the legislation before the House? 1 do not know how. It must have been in their complete absence of mind or exhaustion, because theirs was the ultimate responsibility to keep their eye on those nitwits in the Department of National Revenue who are always trying to extend their power over the people of this country.

That is the only excuse we, as members of parliament, have that we let that clause go through. But everyone of us, having let it go through, should be ashamed, and we in the opposition have to accept that responsibility as well as members of the government.
My remarks to the Minister of Finance are simple. My memory goes back a number of years during the regimes of the last nine finance ministers when I have seen every one of them,

without exception, destroyed, and rarely any one of them was responsible for his own destruction. In each case, with the tremendous responsibility that each one of them had looking after the finances of Canada, the same group which controls the decision-making in that department and in related departments had the minister of finance do things for which he ultimately had to take the responsibility. I have seen them go down since the days of Walter Harris, one after another.
If there is any crusade that I lead in this House, it is not only to protect ministers of finance from the awful fate that lies in wait for them but to protect this House and this parliament in general. So what I say to the minister now is that we in the opposition cannot make an amendment to a bill unless there is a clause in it which would allow us to amend it. The minister cannot do so now either. When we go into committee of the whole I think he would be speaking for every single member on the government side if he put in a simple clause deleting clause 5 regarding SIN in Bill C-22 amending the Income Tax Act. Why do I say that?
When we put through clause 75 under closure it simply said that if any person went into a bank and presented a bond with coupons on it and they did not have with them their SIN, 25 per cent of the value of their coupons would have to be retained by the bank and submitted to the Department of National Revenue, and of course it would be entered as part of the prepayment of their income tax.
Who were the people the Department of National Revenue were after? They were after all the young children who do not have SIN and whose parents bought them $50 or $100 bonds instead of Christmas or birthday presents as savings for the time when they would move into their teens. This also applies to the older people, but above all it applies to the married women who do not have an income of their own, who are not in the work force, and who occasionally get their husbands to buy them a bond. That coupon clipping that they do once a year is equivalent to what we used to have on the farm years ago when the farmer allowed the wife to take the money she got from selling eggs-the egg money, they called it. They used to collect enough money that way to buy Christmas presents for their family.
Here you have these minute searches after minute drops of water and drops of blood. Sneaking through past the politician into the statute books of this country was a clause last February causing a situation we now have to clean up.
There are other points that I could raise, such as the attempt to force the banks to do the dirty work of National Revenue. This did not pass unnoticed, and I have a letter dated October 6, 1977, from the Canadian Bankers' Association, to which I rarely have access. It states simply:
It is unfair that banks should bear the brunt of reaction of the public against intrusions into their financial affairs.
We can all weep for the banks; they are in the firing line. Later on from another gentleman in this same organization I

November 17, 1977
Income Tax
received a copy of a press release sent out by the banks on this same matter. Incidentally, this is from a Toronto bank. It says:
SIN pays. Or at least, it may be inconvenient if you don't have it.
In this case, SIN refers to a Social Insurance number. Starting soon, you'll need one to get the full amount due when you collect certain bond interest payments from banks and other financial institutions.
The Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) issued this caution today, following confirmation that regulations embodied in amendments to the federal Income Tax Act will be effective from July 1.
The CBA said customers who hold corporate, federal, provincial and municipal bonds and who don't have a Social Insurance number, would be wise to apply for one now to avoid future inconvenience. It normally takes at least two weeks to get a number.
The regulations specify that banks and other cashing agents must withhold one quarter of the interest payment if the customer doesn't provide a Social Insurance number. This is remitted to the government and is credited to the taxpayer.
"We want to make it clear that in this matter the banks are acting to comply with the law", the CBA said. "We have no choice but to withhold the 25 per cent if a Social Insurance number is not provided".
I could go on and read letter after letter from individuals, and I may read one or two of them, but I am more interested in the battle that went on in the press as to who was going to take the blame for this.
I will quote now from a full page ad in the Montreal Gazette dated September 21 under the subject "Important News about Canada Savings Bonds". Who do you suppose put this ad out? It was the Department of Finance. Who do you suppose got the blame? The Minister of Finance. He did not even know it went out. The government wants us to buy bonds. We are in a deficit position. Let me put this on the record, loudly and clearly. In big letters its says:
Your social insurance number is important. This year, your social insurance number will be requested when you purchase Canada Savings Bonds. This number will provide accurate identification of your Canada Savings Bond account and will be a single lifetime account number for you no matter how many bonds you buy or when you buy them. It will thus enable the Bank of Canada to provide you with better and faster service in the event that you write to inquire about the status of your bonds.
The people who drafted these ads were telling the people that, according to the statute, they have to have their social insurance numbers when they go to collect on coupons. They went even further and said that people have to have their social insurance numbers to purchase the bonds. What a bunch of sniping and looking into people's affairs that is! Well, time goes on and the criticism increases.
Just a few days ago, November 14, the Bank of Canada replied. It knew the Department of Finance was catching all the blame, so it came out with a story which it fed to the press through one of its pigeons. According to this paper here are some of the statements it made:
"The social insurance number is a positive and unique identification. No matter how many John Smiths there are, only one of them has that particular number."
The official said the Bank of Canada is adopting a new, highly-computerized system so each person's CSB-holdings can be listed under his or her account number.
You don't have to supply your social insurance number when you buy bonds, "but you have everything to gain and nothing to lose by doing so," the official said ...

That completely contradicts what the Department of Finance was saying. The Department was saying that you have to have them. I suggest that the Bank of Canada rushed into the breach trying to find some rationalization as to why the numbers were needed. The bank gave the examples of all the John Smiths in every telephone book, and of the fellow who lost his bonds in the refrigerator and they went out with the garbage. The only real reason for this new change in our statute law on taxation is that the Department of National Revenue wants to catch that unique person who makes less than $10 on coupon cashing per year, because if your coupons amount to $10 or more the bank always reports that to the department.
The department is after that person who has the colossal gall to put his savings into bonds which yield less than $10 per year, and that person must not be forgotten. If 25 per cent is taken off, that person usually has no income tax papers to make out. Invariably that means that an older person will not get that 25 per cent. The department wants everybody to make out an income tax form. I suggest to the minister that it would not cause any fuss amongst his supporters in the House of Commons on the government side, and all the people on this side will support him, if he stands up in the committee of the whole and says he is prepared to allow a very simple amendment. He would not need any lawyer to draft it. The amendment would simply be that subclause (5) of clause 234 of the Income Tax Act is deleted.

That amendment would get rid of another encroachment on our civil liberties. I have some editorials I was going to read, but I think I will leave that for another occasion because there is another subject to which I would like to bring attention.
I put these ideas forward, hopefully in a constructive manner, because I know that any person holding the job of Minister of Finance must be seriously concerned about the mess our economic situation seems to be in. The Minister of Finance knows that we have a very strong and healthy country, so why does it just go along level as it has been for the two years since we established the so-called anti-inflation controls? The minister must be spending some time thinking about that. He knows that the great majority of people believe that the government is spending too much money. He has done a yeoman-type job over the past years trying to control the spenders in the cabinet, and we have noticed that. However, here we have a situation about which the minister must be aware, and we are all worried about it.
We have today a large number of unemployed. Whether the number is 800,000 or one million is not the point. It is a large number. At the same time we have our plant capacity lying 20 per cent unused all across Canada. This situation is not new or unique. It happens every time we go into a prolonged recession, and it takes a tremendous momentum or a change in momentum to get the situation reversed. Therefore the minister must be worrying about this. He knows that if he does not
November 17, 1977

have some ideas on how to change that, he is going to go the way of every previous minister of finance-out. It is not any matter of satisfaction to me to see some very able people going into that portfolio and getting chewed up, one after the other.
The proposal 1 am putting forward is not original with me or with this country. There is a precedent which has been used, to my knowledge, only in a western country, and only in one. When I read the history of how that was done, I find that it was very unique.
It so happened at that particular time in United States history that President Kennedy was very anxious to be in the forefront of new ideas, and this applied to the financing of the country's affairs. He had working for him in the Economic Council a man by the name of Heller. They, too, had a huge unused labour supply ready and willing to work. They, too, had unused plant capacity, and the federal Government of the United States was operating as the present minister is operating, under a tremendous deficit.
The natural tradition of all the orthodox economists, therefore, who try to keep their two-bits worth before the president and away from Congress, was to get back to the old fashioned way of doing things-simply raise taxes to get more money, or reduce expenditures to balance the budget. One man, Heller, gets the credit for proposing that the best way to balance the budget was not to retrench, go into seclusion and wait for time and events to balance it-as this government has been doing for three years, waiting for the United States economy to recover. He proposed that this unused labour supply, this unused plant capacity, were a great opportunity for a young, virile president to try the idea. His proposition was that with substantial tax reductions in those areas where you could immediately start tremendous activity in the work force and in the plant, you would create enough new wealth and reduce costs to the point where you would get your money back. This is a layman's description of what we call potential budgeting. There was a potential there.
1 will not go through all the activities of the 1962-63 period. In the year 1964, however, President Kennedy allowed himself to be persuaded by his Economic Council even though the federal budget was operating at a great deficit, to reduce taxes in the United States by $10 billion in one year. That would be the equivalent of seven or eight times as much today. When you are already in the hole, $10 billion would seem crazy to the orthodox person who does not want to accept new ideas.
Heller put forth the doctrine that the best, quickest, and most humane way to balance the budget was to get the tax level down on those items that would create an immediate desire to go to work. They did reduce the budget by decreasing taxes in 1964 by $10 billion. The president was assassinated that year and it fell to the lot of President Johnson to receive the great flood of revenue that poured in. The $10 billion in tax reductions was not money that was spent; it was simply money they were not going to take in during the next year. It brought increased revenue because of the number of people
Income Tax
who went to work and the plant capacity that started up again. In that one year it produced revenue of $19 billion.
Instead of ending up in the hole by another $10 billion, because of that imaginative and at that time innovative program, the United States came out with a surplus. As President Johnson said, it was able to pay not only for the great society he talked about but also for the Vietnam war. It turned out that he was wrong. Even the United States could not support both for long. I point that out to the minister because the condition in Canada today is very similar.
The only argument against what I have said is that in Johnson's day and in Kennedy's day there was no indexing of taxes or pensions. You can argue that today these things would reduce the amount that would come in as increased revenue from all these people working. Let me deal with that for a moment.
The type of thing that I would like to see, if this approach were to be followed, is tax reductions for those things that the country needs and wants. I will give examples in a minute. New types of production would be brought into play. It is pretty hard to prove, with people running on margin as they are today, that encouraging them to go out and spend will create jobs because plants are already working under capacity.
If you could find a number of things that this country has to do and wants to do and direct our efforts that way, in every case I think this would not be expenditure of money by the federal treasury but simply the statement that you are not going to take taxes if certain things are done. If this new labour force goes to work and the new plant capacity goes to work, and wages and salaries are going to people who before were drawing unemployment insurance and social welfare, you reduce those costs, and with all those people working and paying income tax, and all the money going through the system with a multiplier effect of two and a half or three, a billion dollars of new industry would generate $2.5 billion to $3 billion of new wealth. The $3 billion of new wealth, with the governments getting 40 per cent of it, would bring in more than the new program.
I know that new wealth is divided among the governments, roughly 40 per cent to the federal government, 40 per cent to the provincial governments and 20 per cent to the smaller governments. The fact remains that if the tax reductions were put on the right items, within one or two years the budget would be balanced. We could then begin to do things to encourage people to spend, and we could put out dividends for the extra amounts of money for payment to provinces or in social services.
I am sure this concept is not new to the minister. 1 am simply reminding him that at this time all the conditions that make potential budgeting work, are present. It will not work if this technique is tried where there is no big labour supply and no extra plant capacity. This is the time to move. This opportunity has been present for the last two or three years, but perhaps this winter is the last chance.

I would now like to suggest to the minister, if he accepts this premise, some things on which taxes could be reduced that would give fast results. I am sure the minister is aware, as are most members, that these days we are moving very quickly toward changing our energy utilization. Documents which project utilization of solar hardware indicate that there is a market right now of $1 billion or $2 billion per year for devices to be used in private homes and office buildings. There is a score of examples.
By the end of this decade I believe that almost every home in Canada will have a heat pump. The cost will be $1,000 to $3,000 for the ordinary home. A heat pump acts as an air conditioner in summer, and pumps heat into the house in winter. They can be manufactured in Canada, and indeed they have been on the market for 50 years. A warehouse in Ottawa is full of heat pumps, all unavailable to people here because it is an American firm waiting for the right time to move into the market in this area.
All through the southern areas of Canada-that covers about 90 per cent of the population-a heat pump would be a good investment. In addition to the hardware, which costs $1,000 to $3,000, there are devices that go along with it for use with solar heat. At the present time the idea of direct solar energy, coming through plates is not too economic. But solar assisted techniques are currently in use by big companies. Governments do not use these techniques because they tend to look at bigger things which cost $200,000 or $300,000.
Referring to little individuals across Canada, some are spending $1,000, $2,000 or $3,000 of their money to take water out of their wells and put it in heat pumps to raise the temperature of the water in order to heat their houses. The water is returned to the well, and is warmed up again. The only cost to those individuals is the capital cost of the heat pumps, and the cost of the electricity to run those pumps, which amounts to approximately $100 a year. This is not something in the dream world five years or ten years away from now. This is being done currently.
Some people use the water from a river or a stream which runs by their houses. Other people use water storage. There is a score of techniques which require a certain amount of hardware in order to change it from one type of heat to another. These are not unproven devices. We have the capacity in our plants now to produce these things in the thousands. The government should distribute that information to Canadians.
The Minister of Finance will have a simple role to play. Since very few people have these heat pumps in Canada, and since only businesses are allowed to buy them today, under the direction of the big companies which produce them, if they are told by the minister that they will be entitled to a 100 per cent write-off for a heat pump against their taxes, within three years every householder in Canada will be struggling to get a heat pump. That indicates how big the market could be. All

these people will not be able to get the pumps, because that many could not be manufactured quickly enough.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to support the comments which have just been made by the hon. member who spoke before me about the hopes he has put in the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). This is the first time I have had the opportunity to take part in a debate on a subsidy motion since he has this portfolio. Therefore, 1 understand that he made considerable efforts to sponsor Bill C-ll which contains some provisions amending the Income Tax Act with the purpose of giving certain tax advantages to revive the economy.
I think that all hon. members in the House agree that this revival is very urgent. I think however that the proposed measures are not sufficient and that the economy will continue to deteriorate in several areas of the country. Mr. Speaker, I shall particularly dwell upon the main points of this bill which will have some impact on the people and on the industries in my area, and on Canadian agriculture. The real per capita income has constantly decreased in the last few years and the individuals are more and more indebted, which puts a very large number of taxpayers in the income-cost of living vice which becomes increasingly tight. These are at least the comments which have been made to us every day by people of the working classes.
A few days ago, the Minister of Finance said he was disappointed to see that the cost of living went up again by 1 per cent. Mr. Speaker, each time the cost of living rises, low-income people have less purchasing power when they should actually have more. However, we see the contrary. I think the price and wage control program is a failure when it comes to prices and profits. On the other hand, wage controls were rather successful, which leaves most wage earners in quite a difficult situation.
If we consider the record of our banking institutions, we realize that they have made more profits than any other industry in the economic field. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself has admitted that fact. I have already quoted him in the House on this matter. I hope you will forgive me for bringing up that subject again, but this time without quoting. If these institutions have managed to increase their profits it is because the control regulations did not have authority over them and because the ceiling for interest rates has been abolished in 1967, and God knows how the profits of these insitutions have gone up during the last ten years. I think this is one of the reasons which has put Canada in such an inflationary economic situation.
Those excessively high rates of interest are responsible for the inflation in the prices of goods and services. Rising prices put Canadian industries in an unfavourable position against competing foreign product imports. Finally, the Canadian

November 17, 1977
Income Tax
Manufacturers Association is aware of this situation. This morning, my colleagues met members of that association who apprised us of their worries about the future, the survival of private enterprise, of small and medium-sized businesses which, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) has stated in this House, are those that provide Canada with 60 per cent of its jobs. Is it any wonder that the rate of unemployment goes up progressively as those businesses have problems and have to lay off employees? If solutions are not found for the short term, while planning over the long term, I am very much afraid the future of a very large number of those small and average businesses is very bleak indeed.
However, we often hear well intentioned people, I hope, claim that inflation is caused mainly by unduly high salaries. That may be true of some categories of workers and professionals who do not hesitate to ask fairly high fees when Canadians turn to them for their services. But I do not agree with blaming price inflation solely on wage earners. A huge number of non-unionized workers now earn less than the minimum wage.
Speaking of the minimum salary, we are told that it is higher here in Canada than in the United States and that this causes problems for the Canadian industries as compared with American firms. That is true, but the fact remains that today a couple with two or three children cannot be asked to work 40 hours a week for $3 an hour. That is $120 gross, and considering the costs those people have to pay just like everyone else- public services, electricity, telephone, heating oil, in short all the basic needs-it cannot be said that those workers are the cause of inflation, of higher prices. Let us be reasonable. It behoves the state, in difficult situations, to introduce measures to straighten out matters in that sector. I understand that it is normal, when a business is expanding, when it wants to create employment, that it deserves to be given every possible chance of doing so.
But if we really are to give them a chance to expand and survive, we must look at the budgetary operations of these companies which must pay very high interest rates, thus increasing their operating costs and becoming less competitive.
I said earlier that the control program had not been a complete success. We are not overly optimistic about the outcome of the recovery program introduced by the Minister of Finance. I understand it has been prepared in a hurry and that the government will perhaps announce more worthwhile measures in the real budget. Life is made of hope. Until then, the new Minister of Finance will certainly have the opportunity to get to the root of the matter and, as the previous speaker said, to twist the arms of those whom may wish to maintain old formulas and to keep on administering in 1977 as we did 25 or 30 years ago. In the Speech from the Throne, we are told this was a failure and that we should use more modern processes. I hope that in the new budget we shall have up-dated and more modern formulas which will enable us to hope for an improved situation.

The thousands of unemployed who are now hoping are quite prepared to work, thus contributing to the recovery of our economy. We should at least give them the chance to do it. Before I came to the House tonight, the mayor of a municipality spoke to me on the phone for some 20 minutes, and he insisted so that the very well prepared and organized project that he put forward under the program Canada at Work be accepted and implemented in order to give work to the unemployed of his community as early as possible. Of course, I have also commended this project because I think it is worthwhile. Those people are making fantastic efforts, they do practical things, but when there are $3.5 million worth of projects for a budget of only $1,159,000, some of them of course have to be shelved.
This is why I am asking and suggesting to the Minister of Finance, along with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), that more funds be made available to the Department of Employment so that it can sponsor a larger number of worthwhile projects. I am not dealing with meaningless projects; I am speaking only of good projects which do something useful, those projects which please the whole community and from which everybody can benefit.
Mr. Speaker, the tax concessions provided in this bill are there to allow companies to invest more money in Canada and create new jobs. I fully agree with that but I think we will have to exert some surveillance over these companies. I fear that more money will just disappear in the long run, that it will take some other direction. The recent behaviour of INCO and Noranda Mines Limited, to talk only about those two, clearly demonstrates that these large corporations do not give a heck about reinvesting in the country. They prefer to reinvest their money in other countries, looking down their nose at Canadians. This is where the government's authority intervenes. The government must take radical steps, if necessary, to force the companies that have been allowed to make profits here to reinvest these profits in Canada in order to help with more development and enable us to keep up with competition. I have a suggestion to make to the Minister of Finance: I think that rebates made on real investments in Canada might be much more indicated. Of course, these partial rebates could be calculated according to the number of jobs created.
There would then be a reaction between capital and manpower resources. In this optic, I believe that the amendments aimed at increasing tax credits for investment are a step in the right direction. The higher credit percentages for the designated areas should stimulate investments in these areas and contribute to reduce regional disparities. There is no doubt that the Maritimes and the Gaspe peninsula need these special stimulants.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the region which neighbours on the Maritime provinces and the Gaspe peninsula, that is the south shore and east shore of Quebec. The economic situation in the Bellechasse and Kamouraska ridings is far from favourable. Among the many characteristics that these areas have in common,
November 17, 1977

there is unfortunately a very high rate of unemployment. This is why I invite the Minister of Finance to reconsider clause 127(10) of the bill so that the definition of areas eligible for the 10 per cent tax credit for investment be extended to include, in addition to the Maritime provinces, the south shore east of Highway 23 which links Levis to the state of Maine. Indeed, this is the area covered by the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act. Therefore, such an amendment would simply correspond to existing legislation.
For this region to survive and to develop normally, it must be provided with economic advantages by the federal and provincial governments. Why not grant tax rebates on fuel used by businesses which operate on diesel engines?
Mr. Speaker, I have a letter sent to me by a medium size business which echoes its concerns about the rising costs of transportation. I wish to quote from it as I consider this letter very timely and it demonstrates that it is only after consultation with those businesses that I make those comments. So I am told, and I quote:
I respectfully draw your attention on some data concerning the trucking business. We employ between 35 and 50 employees annually, all depending on the transportation industry. We are a medium size enterprise but, nevertheless, hundreds of farm producers of the southern Quebec area depend on us as to transport cattle to the slaughter-houses.
And the operations of those slaughter houses depend on the quantity of animals we deliver to them and so they directly depend on transportation. It means that our service can be considered as vital for the society and the economy of the area. The taxes we pay and the share paid by other transportation firms contribute to a large extent to the construction and use of highways in our area and the province.
As a result, transportation firms are paying more than their share of registration costs but the government would like to increase that share ...
I understand that this part of the letter concerns the provincial government.
... believing that it is insufficient. Is it its intention to reduce the number of trucks on highways or their economic contribution to each area of the province?
The important point is this:
If transportation firms must reduce their number of trucks due to the excessive cost of...
-everything they must use in their operations-
... it will eliminate many jobs and in some cases those employment losses will affect the economy of a town, of an area depending almost exclusively on that industry.
Mr. Speaker, it is not for nothing that earlier I asked that the possibility of lowering the tax on the fuel used in diesel engines be considered again, be it in the case of industries using stationary engines or in the case of big trucking firms.
I also wish to ask the government to show greater understanding towards depressed areas. It is not our fault if Canada is big and not very populated. This means that all across this country there are Canadians who live and have the right to like their regions but who would rather enjoy former living standards. This is why we have a government, namely to make it easier for all Canadians to enjoy a decent standard of living geared to the economic potential of Canada. Who else than the
Income Tax
government can do better to try and establish equity between all regions of the country? These regions, such as the south shore, are not progressing at the same pace as Montreal for example. Yet, we have a human capital quite capable of achieving more than it is presently doing. The number of unemployed is quite high and it is sad to witness such a waste of human energy. There is talk about increasing productivity in Canada. These are the kind of energies that could contribute to higher productivity but no steps are taken to use them efficiently.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I will act as a member from the opposition who is not obsessed only with showing his opposition. When something good is done, I do not mind saying so. I would therefore like to take the opportunity to thank the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) whom I scolded a good many times in the past, and whom I want to thank tonight as well as his colleague from Public Works (Mr. Buchanan) for the restoration of the Montmagny wharf. 1 had so often talked about it in this House that it had become a rather embarrassing subject to raise. But, in any event, the matter has been given consideration, the works are in progress and the population is generally satisfied as I am happy to report. I would also like to thank the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) for what is now taking place on Berthier's wharf. A long boat slip is being installed and will be used not only for the benefit of the people of Berthier but by any member of this House who will decide to visit my riding, as I invite them to do. Berthier's wharf is beautiful and now with this long boat slip things will be just fine.
Again I am pressing the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard). And I do not intend to give up-

We are talking about Quebec. We are told that we do not have our share. When we do I like to say so. When we do not I like to say so as well.
I am asking the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to prepare a specific project for the south shore, within the framework of the Ottawa-Quebec agreements. This region would be recognized as a special area within which we would promote the development of existing industries and the establishment of new plants to absorb a large pool of skilled local labour. I am sorry when I see that the only thing available for those big healthy boys who have been studying or who have a trade is social welfare, not even unemployment insurance, because never having had the opportunity to work they cannot even draw unemployment benefits.
The situation is really serious and if we are not dealing with it now I think we will regret it. This is true not only for the south shore region but for other regions as well. I would like to deal with another aspect of the question, the "employment

Income Tax
expenses deduction" which used to be $150 and is now to be raised to $250.
This is a very good start, but in fact it is much below the real costs. Travel expenses alone top the new amount, especially in rural or semi-rural areas where people are often faced with a 40-, 50- or 60-mile commuting distance. The worker who has to commute over those 40 miles has to spend more than $450 a year. In my view, the maximum deduction should be increased by at least $200. Unemployment is severe enough already without penalizing those who are working. They also deserve attention.
And while on the subject of penalties, I would like to stress how ridiculous clause 6(5) is, subjecting the $350 home insulation grant to income tax. A number of members in this House already felt such an initiative was absurd. As far as I am concerned I feel it is very worthwhile, provided taxpayers can take advantage of it. But in the province of Quebec we cannot, and I once more urge the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) to press for and accelerate negotiations between officials from both levels of government, so we can one day give an answer to those who would like to take advantage of the program, telling them, yes everything is settled, they can file their applications, have the work done and get paid. I feel I am being very positive and I would like officials to take note of our remarks. We are not fighting them, all we ask is that they find ways, formulas so that Quebecers like all other Canadians may take advantage of that initiative.
Mr. Speaker, there is one way to promote consumer spending, because it has been said, and rightly so, that in some areas consumer spending is too low. We came forward not so long ago with a proposal for a retail discount. I shall amplify that next week if the bill I introduced in this House is called for debate in the course of next week.
Finally, I would call the minister's attention to the possible adverse impact of capital gains tax and I ask once more that the Minister of Finance review that policy. In recent years, acting on an idea by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), a number of family farms were incorporated. It is true that advantages outweigh disadvantages, but the forecasts for capital gains tax will likely put an end to these advantages by unjustly penalizing the father who sells his farm to his son. Even if these farms have been given a corporate status, we should not forget that they nevertheless remain family farms. That is why I would ask the minister to reconsider these measures so that family farms are not subjected to such disadvantages.
In conclusion, I would like to emphasize the urgency of adopting truly stimulating measures for the economy. It is not only in the interest of our own welfare but for the welfare of the young generations. They should not have to pay for our failures and those of our present leaders. If this government cannot solve the serious problems facing it, how will we be able tomorrow to condemn their apathy, even their cynicism towards our institutions.
I urge all members and ministers to see to the implementation of that part of the throne speech which was read by Her

Majesty the Queen on October 18 last and who said that it was absolutely necessary if we wanted to emerge from chaos to resort to new formulas. The cabinet which is responsible should seriously listen to the suggestions of hon. members, whatever the side from which they originate. I think we are all seriously working together to improve the economy to the country, to settle the problems which are disrupting harmony in Canada.
At times we refer to national unity, at others, to national harmony; I feel it is nicer to speak about harmony. It means a little more love for one another and I think it is the only way to ensure the survival of our country, of Canada as we know it. We need formulas to promote that harmony and if we take care we will attain that aim and the future generations will be happy and pleased with us.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is appropriate that I begin my remarks in this debate by saying that surely it must be considered as a dual capacity type of debate because it not only deals with actual income tax amendments but it also serves as a budget debate. That was not possible after the minister's mini-budget speech during the throne debate.
I find it indeed strange that our Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) should have sent out a news release the day after the debate began-I believe it was November 8-urging all members to avoid unnecessary delay in proceeding with it, after the same kind of bill in the last session, Bill C-56, for the budget of last spring, was given first reading only last June 15 and then was never called for second reading debate during the last session. So this new bill, Bill C-11, which we are debating all of this week, is indeed more than doubly important to all Canadians. My remarks tonight will relate primarily to those aspects of the bill pertaining to small businesses, including agriculture, with special reference to the Canadian cattle industry.
Almost three years ago I took part in the same kind of debate, both on second reading and in committee of the whole. That was on February 4 and February 18, 1975. At that time my remarks concentrated on the impact of the capital gains tax on incorporated family farms and farm partnerships. You will remember that the new approach to our tax structure involving capital gains had started on January 1, 1972.
During that earlier debate, the minister of the day-of course it was Mr. Turner-denied any possibility of roll-over tax provisions that were permitted for individual farm operators for intergenerational transfers of ownership in incorporated family farms and partnerships. I want to take another look at this issue today, almost three years later, and I suggest this is certainly the time for another look at this very important aspect of present-day agriculture under existing tax laws.
Incorporated family farms account for a disproportionately large share of Canadian farm production. Seven per cent of
November 17, 1977

our Canadian farms are incorporated, but they account for 28 per cent of total farm production, and this does not include partnerships. Why did they incorporate in the first place, particularly 15, 20 and 25 years ago? The fundamental reason was to enhance and preserve the family farm as a continuing and meaningful farm unit. Now the exact opposite is taking place, that is, the breaking up of family farm units due to the inescapable requirements of the capital gains provisions for corporate and partnership farms.
In those earlier days governments, both provincial and federal, actively promoted farm incorporations. Then you will recall the Carter Tax Commission. It recommended incorporation for certain size farms, usually the larger size. Perhaps the most immediate reason that appealed to farmers themselves was that wives and family members could be legally involved and paid for their services on the family farm. Our Income Tax Act, as amended back in 1975, as I said, and again now as proposed in this bill, is still not adequate with respect to capital gains tax provisions for incorporated family farms, small businesses, and partnerships.
I want to begin by presenting three specific case histories of actual family farm corporations. All of these have very serious problems involved in a proposed intergenerational transfer because of the inadequacies of our federal tax laws. While these case histories deal with farms and ranches that are larger than average, I suggest the same problems exist for much smaller incorporated family businesses and partnerships.
The first case history is a fairly large cattle ranch in western Canada. It is operated by the third and fourth generation in the same family on the same cattle ranch, and there is a fifth generation well on the way. This cattle ranch has been placed on the market. It was advertised for sale quite recently. It has a value of somewhere between $3 million and $3.5 million. The ranch was incorporated in 1957, that is, 20 years ago. In that interval land values in the area have increased from four to four and a half times. The fourth generation would have a tax liability of three quarters of a million dollars, and the yearly interest on that tax alone is some $75,000. So far there has been very little interest in the advertisements of the sale of this ranch, especially from Canada or the United States. However, there are some prospects from European sources.
This particular family, composed of very studious and capable people I can assure you, reasons that they have no other choice except to sell out. The debt load for the fourth generation is impossible to work out, even over a generation, and particularly after the last three disastrous cattle market years. So we have the incredible prospect of a fourth and fifth generation Canadian farmer being displaced by foreign owners and operators with foreign capital.
The second case history involves another unit in western Canada. This one is a mixed grain and cattle operation that operates on both irrigated and dry land in the western prairies. Two family units are involved in this one operation. It is incorporated, of course, and it contains approximately 9,000 acres. Its assets today total approximately $2.5 million, and the total tax liability, if it is offered for sale or if the capital
Income Tax
gains tax comes into play, will be again three quarters of a million dollars.
This family unit that is incorporated wishes to move to two separate family farm corporations. To do so they require a form of reverse amalgamation to roll out the assets of the parent company to the new family units. Again, as in case one, they are faced with the almost impossible debt load which will result from the capital gains tax.
This family unit began with two succeeding and different partnerships which operated from 1945 to 1952, and this was followed by a single limited company which was set up in 1961. Now they find there is no room for members of the next generation, which happens to be the third generation to farm under this corporate structure. The problem in this one is not a transfer of assets from one generation to the next but a roll out of existing assets of a single company to two new companies involving the present family shareholders. To do so, the decision to divide in 1975, and that is when they made this decision, requires the process that I mentioned which might be called reverse amalgamation, with provision in the Income Tax Act to permit such a division. Of course, that does not exist now.
The third case history is a ! ,000 acre beef farm in the province of Ontario. It involves two family units, each with a son ready to take over what they hope will be a new family corporate set-up, changing from a single incorporated farm unit to two separate incorporated family units. The single unit was incorporated in 1962. Land values in this case have increased considerably since valuation day, but not as dramatically as the two previous examples from western Canada which I gave. In spite of a half million dollar operating loss due to the disastrous cattle price year of 1976, capital gains tax in this case for only a half share in this family unit is well in excess of $100,000, but the total amount is not yet finalized.
In all three case histories I have reflected on certain severe inadequacies of the income tax which have become quite apparent. Our income tax laws in Canada are responsible in their application for these severe limitations.
Two of the three cases involve intergenerational roll-overs to the next generation, and one requires a division of the existing family corporate structure into two or possibly more family corporations in anticipation of an intergenerational transfer later on. In all three cases none of the families wanted to stop farming or sell out completely. All wished to continue in the same family line. All were incorporated before the start of the new tax policy involving capital gains, which started back on January 1, 1972.
All three cases are in severe difficulties because of the dramatic increase in agricultural land values which has occurred since 1971. Why this great increase in land values? That is at the root of this, plus the interpretation of our tax laws. There are a number of reasons. One is the real increase in farmland values resulting mainly from the re-investment of profits to improve productivity. Another one is the increasing scarcity of farmland, especially in Ontario, British Columbia

November 17, 1977
Income Tax
and, I presume, in Manitoba. However, even now on the prairies this is becoming more and more a factor. Finally, there is the insidious impact of inflation, the most important reason, and this includes the substantial amount of nonagricultural financing invested in our farmlands as a hedge against inflation. I think this is by far the most important reason why we have seen land values increase so dramatically. A combination of these three major factors has caused farmland values to increase anywhere from two to four and a half times, going back seven years, or since the advent of the capital gains tax.
In all three case histories the best available accountants, tax experts, and estate planners were employed for their expert advice by the respective families. The transfer of shares in a family farm company to a son in the event of a death of course results in an immediate realization of capital gains. Tax payments can be spread over several years, but the tax cannot be avoided; hence the increasing number of forced sales, such as that first case history to which I referred, to satisfy the capital gains tax.
While these remarks have all related to incorporated family farm situations, the same can be said for incorporated small family businesses of a non-farm nature. However, we should keep in mind that the capital needs in agriculture as a ratio of gross and net income are much higher than in other small business pursuits, indicating a disproportionate need for a tax roll-over provision for the corporate family farm. This is fully documented in a report of the Food Prices Review Board of March, 1975. This particular report shows that the investment ratio to gross domestic product in agriculture is well over twice as large as the same ratio in manufacturing. The report also finds that investment in land and buildings of Canadian farmers constitutes 70 per cent of the total capital value per farm.
I want now to go back to that earlier reference to the debate on the income tax amendments almost three years ago during Mr. Turner's period as Minister of Finance. I refer to Hansard of February 18, 1975, and also to the proceedings of the committee of the whole. In response to my arguments favouring roll-over provisions for incorporated family farms and partnerships, Mr. Turner had this to say as reported at page 3331:
We were concerned about persuading more people to stay on the land and produce food. We recognized the difficulty in respect of a family farm in the current economic structure, and we eliminated the capital gains tax on the transformation of a family farm from one generation to another as long as the land remains in agricultural use. The difficulty is that since the land is so illiquid, the payment of capital gains tax on the value of the land is very difficult, particularly in those areas of the country where there might be an artificial effect as a result of suburban sprawl. In this event the land is drawn out of agricultural production because the children cannot raise the money to pay the tax on the death of the father or mother, and it is the land, that is liquidated.
In the case of an incorporated farm there is not that type of liquidity because the shares, by reason of estate planning, can be transmitted over a period of time within the lifetime of the father and mother, and the same problem of liquidity does not arise.

A little later he said:
On the question raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, there is very little logic in segregating the incorporated family farm as a business from any other incorporated business in the country-of which there are hundreds of thousands-so that in fairness, if one were to allow capital gains, free transmission from one generation to another in an incorporated family farm, there would be little argument for resisting that transmission on a tax free basis from one generation to another in any incorporated family business.
With respect to Mr. Turner's last point about the inclusion of any-that means all-incorporated family business for the roll-over provision, I say most emphatically, why not? If ever there was a time in our history when small family style businesses of all kinds needed a shot in the arm it is certainly now when there is such widespread concern over the state of our economy. There is no question we are in a prolonged recession; it is just a matter of definition as to how serious it is. Small family businesses are the backbone of our Canadian way of life. If Britain's strength during the war was part and parcel of being a nation of shopkeepers, then Canada's strength and future relate directly to our private enterprise system and incentive for the small family business. They must have a sure future, including a reasonable process to continue that business, especially as an incorporated family business.
Mr. Turner's comments suggest that a liquidity problem would not exist with estate planning, that is, for incorporated family farms. This is simply not so, and I have already advanced some solid reasons for that. While it is possible for some kinds of estate freezing plans to defer taxes on capital gains until the death of the father, absolute avoidance is, of course, impossible, particularly where the rate of appreciation in value is considerable, which is certainly so now under our continued severe inflation.
Mr. Turner was concerned also about adequately defining a family farm corporation. There are a variety of definitions readily available. I should like to remind the House of three such sources: first, the federal government's Farm Credit Act which defines a family corporation; second, the Ontario government's gift tax act and succession duty act; and third, the British Columbia succession duty act. It should be noted the two Ontario definitions make no distinction between farming corporations and other small business corporations, and further, Ontario recognizes as an adequate definition of a small business the definition provided in section 125 of the Income Tax Act.
To conclude these remarks about capital gains and intergenerational roll-over for incorporated family businesses and partnerships, surely it is obvious some of our tax laws must be modified or changed. Seven years after valuation day and the Carter Commission, surely it is time to recognize what disasters are built into our tax structure and are only now becoming obvious because of the ravages of inflation.
Let us take a look at what can be done in this regard. First,
I suggest the easiest, most important and basic solution is to allow the same roll-over provisions for incorporated family farms and partnerships as for the individual units now pro-
November 17, 1977

vided for by statute. Second, let us recognize that some incorporated family arrangements, which were established before valuation day, must now be entitled to a reverse amalgamation process. I have referred to that in the second case history which I cited. Third, why not give serious consideration to a new valuation day which would be much closer to present-day circumstances? Fourth, we could always examine the experiences and tax provisions in the United States where the intergenerational transfer principle has been available for some time now, provided the new generation stays in the business for a reasonable time frame. This is the principle of capital gains forgiveness, as distinct from the roll-over principle.
This principle is recognized already in Ontario and British Columbia succession duty legislation. A condition for such existing legislation is that the new generation continue to operate the farm for at least a ten year period, which is a sensible and reasonable provision. If a specific time frame presents administrative problems, perhaps a more general once-in-a-lifetime roll-over provision could be permitted.
Before leaving this subject, I want to remind the House, during this important debate, that the recent Commission of Inquiry into the Marketing of Beef and Veal received widespread input comment on this subject during their nation-wide hearings. As a result, their recommendation No. 14 reads as follows:
The deferral of capital gains tax, as it now applies to the family farm should be extended to cover family farming corporations.
It did not mention partnerships, but 1 am sure that the commission would want to include partnerships in that recommendation.
On a philosophical note, 1 would remind all parties concerned over this tax item that farmers, especially western farmers, have traditionally reinvested their profits, at least most of them, back into their farms and ranches for many generations. This no doubt developed as an aftermath of western pioneer days and, more particularly, as a result of ten years of drought and depression in the thirties.
That was followed by at least another ten years of adjusting to an agricultural economy when farmers had to learn all over again how to use financing and how to use cash money. An entire generation of farmers were affected in this way. It was as a consequence of this phase of western farm history that the observation has often been made that farmers, especially cattlemen, are broke most of the time without knowing it, but very often end up the richest men in the graveyard. There is a very obvious update to that quote today. Capital gains taxation has brought about an abrupt end to that continuing possibility.
I would like to make some appropriate remarks about another aspect of western agriculture that has a direct relationship with the income tax amendment. I am referring to the matter of the continuing and worsening drought across southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan. This House has heard me comment on this subject over the past year on a
Income Tax
number of occasions. I suppose it is a sort of labour of love, if one can really love a disaster. After all, the recent news stories of excessive rain in western Canada and the serious threat to our grain harvest, which is now over, most people, especially here in central Canada, assumed that the western drought was over. I must say that over much of the straight grain producing areas it is over, but all across southern Alberta, except, our irrigation areas, and the entire southwest part of Saskatchewan, the serious drought continues and worsens.
We have now had in this area three winter droughts and two summer droughts. In severity, they are at least the equivalent of the three worst years of the thirties, at least as I remember them. That was 1931, 1932 and 1937. That is with respect to soil moisture or more properly, the lack of soil moisture. However, the surface water situation that is needed for stock watering is much worse, the worst I have ever seen.
The cabinet committee of eight ministers that was formed early this year, with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), as chairman, was established last spring as a direct consequence of this widespread and serious western drought.
At various times I was concerned enough to make specific recommendations to this committee and its Regina task force. My personal letters of May 10, June 28, August 11 and, more recently, November 3 are a matter of record. The last one dated November 3 went to the Minister of Finance. I am genuinely pleased to report that a number of my suggestions have been acted upon. But perhaps my most important suggestion, a tax deferral provision, has not been accepted and it would appear it has been rejected.
A fundamental fact of farm life we learned during the drought of the 1930's was that the prudent course to follow was to reduce the number of our cattle, mostly cows, to a level which could be supported on our depleted winter ranges, augmented by local feed supplies, and then to buy back in, or, more often, to grow back in by natural increase after the period of drought was over. This might take years, but in 1977 it is still the prudent thing to do.
Starting a year ago now, cattle have been reduced in number to a considerable extent, and many more will have to move in the course of the next two months in numbers well above normal fall culling. There is no panic selling. After three or four years of disastrous cattle prices the market upturn is now well established. All categories of cattle are selling approximately $10 a hundredweight above levels of a year ago.
There is a very significant difference between this drought and the drought of the thirties. There was no income tax then. Cattle producers had no need to concern themselves about excessively high taxable incomes due to much larger cattle sales. They do now, of course. It just does not make sense to feed hay at $75 to $80 a ton to a $200 cow for five or six months. It will be a long, hard winter, regardless of how mild temperatures may be, because of severely depleted winter grass and feed reserves. Twice the value of a cow could easily

November 17, 1977
Income Tax
be fed during the feeding period this winter. Drastic reduction of cattle numbers is the right course to follow. Cattlemen know this, but they are very concerned about the tax position which would obviously result from much higher taxable incomes, in some cases as much as 50 per cent to 100 per cent higher than in more normal years.
A major incentive for cattlemen to do what they know is right, that is, to reduce the numbers of their herds, would be the introduction of a tax deferral plan along lines which have been well documented and presented to the cabinet drought committee and the tax policy branch of the Department of Finance. Such a plan would have to continue, not only until the drought was over but until grass and feed supplies return to normal. That may take years. Remember the lesson of the thirties.
This tax deferral plan has been fully supported by the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan and I have reason to believe that the tax policy branch of the Department of Finance itself has given it some support. Unfortunately, it would seem that it is the Minister of Agriculture who has rejected the proposal. He has suggested that cattle herds are being reduced only to normal levels and that this is the conclusion reached by a drought task force survey last summer. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, this is not so. 1 say this most emphatically. Further, 1 would call attention to the response given to me by the Minister of Agriculture that there is "a rational culling of breeding herds which will serve to bring herd sizes more in line with normal range-carrying capacity."
Mr. Speaker, we simply do not have normal range-carrying capacity at the present time. Our carrying capacity in the drought area is the worst since 1937, which is 40 years ago, and I have been involved in the cattle industry in the heart of that drought area for every one of those 40 years, excepting the war years. In many cases cattle numbers have already been reduced by one half-in my own case it is by one third-and further reductions over the entire drought area will be necessary during the next two months.
I ask the special cabinet drought committee of eight, including the Minister of Finance, with the Minister of Agriculture
as chairman, to reconsider the advisability of this tax deferral proposal. It is reasonable and practical; it has very wide support and it could serve as a last resort which would allow cattle producers to survive in a critical drought area. I am sure the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), and the Minister of State for the Environment (Mr. Mar-chand) are fully conversant with both the subjects of which I speak tonight.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a very brief comment on the cancellation of the plans to tax life insurance policies in the hands of the recipient. I do so because of the heavy mail I have received, and I am sure every member in this House has received somewhat similar mail. This is the main reason the minister, in his good judgment, withdrew the major portions of that bill. I also think we should seriously consider doing away with the other two aspects proposed in that bill, the one on the alleged investment element at the time of a policy loan and the other one, of course, which disallows deduction of interest paid on policy loans.
I am looking forward to the committee stage when Bill C-l 1 comes before us for discussion in detail, and I hope to participate at that time on the matters which I have raised.
Finally, the father in one of those case histories which I referred to, when I was discussing the details over the telephone, after I am sure a very difficult day at home on his ranch, had this to say after discussing his critical farm situation, "We can handle the cattle physically; we can live with the weather under all circumstances, but when the bureaucrats and politicians move in after four years of depressed markets, what chance have we got?"
